questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the need for doctrine beyond philosophy?
options: Philosophy alone is enough for salvation.
Revelation is unnecessary for understanding God.
A sacred science must be taught by revelation.
Only faith, not knowledge, matters.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says a divine revelation is needed beyond human reason for salvation.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say revelation is necessary?
options: Because faith alone suffices to know God.
Because reason alone would take too long and be error‑prone.
Because revelation replaces philosophy entirely.
Because philosophy already covers all truths about God.
questions.explanation: He argues reason would discover truths slowly and with errors, so revelation is needed for sure salvation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1 about seeking beyond reason?
options: He says revelation is unnecessary because reason suffices.
He claims philosophy already covers all needed knowledge.
He says those beyond reason must be accepted by faith once revealed.
He agrees that nothing beyond reason should be sought.
questions.explanation: His reply states that things beyond reason must be accepted by faith when revealed.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether sacred doctrine is a single science?
options: It is one science only in name, but practically functions as multiple distinct philosophical disciplines.
It is a collection of separate sciences, each handling a different type of creature or moral issue.
It is not one science because it deals with vastly different subjects like God and physical creatures.
It is one unified science because all its subjects share the common feature of being divinely revealed.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states 'Sacred doctrine is one science' and argues that its unity comes from viewing all subjects under the single aspect of divine revelation.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what specific factor makes sacred doctrine a single, unified science?
options: The fact that it examines all subjects under the single perspective of being divinely revealed.
The fact that it combines insights from various existing philosophical sciences into one system.
The fact that it focuses primarily on God, treating creatures only in relation to Him.
The fact that it deals exclusively with spiritual beings like angels, ignoring physical matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the unity of a science is determined by the 'formality' of its object; here, that formality is 'being divinely revealed,' which unifies all topics discussed.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that sacred doctrine cannot be one science because it treats both God and creatures?
options: He states that creatures are merely illusions, so the science actually deals only with God.
He argues that God and creatures are actually the same class of subjects when viewed spiritually.
He admits the objection is correct but argues that practical necessity overrides this logical problem.
He claims that sacred doctrine treats God primarily, and creatures only as they relate to God.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the science is not impaired because it treats God primarily and creatures only insofar as they are referable to God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about whether sacred doctrine is a practical science?
options: It is neither speculative nor practical, but a unique third category.
It is practical because it is divided into the Old and New Laws.
It is purely practical because its main goal is to guide human behavior.
It is primarily speculative, though it also includes practical elements.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that sacred doctrine is speculative rather than practical because it focuses more on divine things than human acts, even though it treats human acts in relation to knowing God.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for classifying sacred doctrine as more speculative than practical?
options: It commands people to be doers of the word, not just hearers.
It is divided into two distinct parts, the Old and New Law.
It deals with divine matters more than with human actions.
It is based on the authority of the Philosopher's Metaphysics.
questions.explanation: The text explicitly says it is speculative because it is 'more concerned with divine things than with human acts.'

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that sacred doctrine is practical because it is divided into the Old and New Law?
options: He rejects the premise that law implies a practical science.
He states that sacred doctrine includes both speculative and practical aspects.
He claims the Old and New Laws are purely speculative topics.
He argues that being divided into laws makes it a moral science only.
questions.explanation: In his answer, Aquinas explains that sacred doctrine is one science that extends to different areas, including both speculative and practical matters, which addresses the objection about its division into laws.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nobility of sacred doctrine compared to other sciences?
options: It is equal to other sciences because both depend on the same level of logical proof.
It is nobler than practical sciences but less noble than speculative sciences like mathematics.
It is less noble than philosophy because it relies on human reason which can make mistakes.
It is nobler than all other sciences because it surpasses them in certainty and subject matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that sacred doctrine transcends all other sciences, both speculative and practical, due to its superior certainty and the higher worth of its subject matter.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is the certainty of sacred doctrine superior to that of other sciences?
options: It depends on the authority of ancient philosophers who never made logical errors.
It is more certain because it deals with everyday things that are easy to observe.
It is based on divine knowledge which cannot be misled, unlike human reason which can err.
It avoids doubt entirely by using mathematical principles that are impossible to question.
questions.explanation: The text explains that other sciences derive certainty from human reason, which is fallible, whereas sacred doctrine derives its certainty from divine knowledge, which is infallible.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that sacred doctrine seems less certain because its principles can be doubted?
options: He claims that the principles of faith cannot actually be doubted by anyone with a good mind.
He states that sacred doctrine is less certain but still valuable for moral guidance.
He suggests that philosophical sciences are also doubtful, so they are equally uncertain.
He argues that human intelligence is too weak to grasp the truth, like an owl dazzled by the sun.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas uses the analogy of an owl being dazzled by the sun to explain that what is truly certain may appear less certain to us due to the limitations of our own understanding.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether sacred doctrine is the same as wisdom?
options: It is distinct from wisdom, which is acquired only through divine inspiration.
It is a lower form of wisdom limited to specific human tasks like building.
It is not wisdom because it relies on principles borrowed from other sources.
It is the highest form of wisdom because it deals with God as the supreme cause.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because sacred doctrine treats of God, the highest cause of the universe, it is wisdom above all human wisdom.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for calling sacred doctrine 'wisdom'?
options: It proves the foundational principles of all other academic sciences.
It focuses on practical advice for daily human life and prudence.
It judges all things by the highest principle, which is God.
It is learned through study rather than through divine inspiration.
questions.explanation: Aquinas defines wisdom as judging by the highest principle; since sacred doctrine considers God as the absolute highest cause, it is truly wisdom.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that sacred doctrine is not wisdom because it borrows its principles?
options: He argues it borrows principles from human philosophy, which is sufficient.
He states it derives principles from divine knowledge, the highest wisdom.
He admits it borrows principles but says wisdom does not require originality.
He claims it does not borrow principles but discovers them through natural reason.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that sacred doctrine derives its principles from divine knowledge, not human knowledge, thus maintaining its status as wisdom.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether sacred doctrine is a matter of argument?
options: It is a matter of argument, but only from faith, not from reason.
It is a matter of argument, but only from philosophical science.
It is not a matter of argument at all.
It is a matter of argument, but only from authority.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says sacred doctrine is a matter of argument, but the argument comes from faith (authority), not from human reason.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say sacred doctrine can argue from faith?
options: Because faith provides principles that can be used to prove other truths.
Because the Holy Scriptures are the only source of truth.
Because reason cannot prove any truth, so faith must do it.
Because faith is infallible, so arguments from faith are always true.
questions.explanation: He explains that doctrines do not prove their own principles; they use those principles to prove other truths, like the resurrection.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1 that sacred doctrine is not a matter of argument?
options: He says the objection is correct but only for certain doctrines.
He agrees, saying faith cannot be argued.
He says faith is the only source of argument, so the objection is irrelevant.
He says the objection is wrong because faith can be used to argue for other truths.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that although human reason cannot prove what must be received on faith, the doctrine argues from articles of faith to other truths.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the use of metaphors in Holy Scripture?
options: Scripture should avoid metaphors to keep its status as the highest science distinct from poetry.
Scripture should only use metaphors derived from the highest and most noble creatures.
Scripture should use metaphors to make divine truths accessible to human understanding.
Scripture should use metaphors primarily to entertain readers with pleasing literary representations.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that it is fitting for Scripture to use comparisons with material things because human knowledge begins with the senses, making metaphors necessary for understanding spiritual truths.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why Scripture uses metaphors?
options: Metaphors prevent the truth from being obscured by being hidden behind sacred veils.
God is too complex to be described directly, so metaphors are the only way to speak of Him.
Using metaphors allows the wise to explain the text to the unwise without error.
Human beings naturally learn intellectual truths through sensory experiences and material objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that it is natural for humans to reach intellectual truths through sensible objects, so spiritual truths are taught through the likeness of material things.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that Scripture should use higher creatures to represent God?
options: The choice of creature depends on the specific historical context of the biblical author.
Using lower creatures helps prevent people from making false assumptions about God's nature.
Lower creatures are more common, so they are easier for simple people to recognize.
Higher creatures are too close to God to serve as useful comparisons for human minds.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas cites Dionysius to say that using less noble bodies helps preserve men's minds from error regarding divine truths.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether words in Holy Scripture can have multiple meanings?
options: Yes, a single word can have multiple senses, even within the literal sense, because God is the author.
No, because the author of Scripture is God, who intends for every word to have exactly one fixed meaning.
No, multiple meanings create confusion and deception, so Scripture must have only one clear sense.
Yes, but only if the multiple meanings are all spiritual and ignore the literal historical meaning.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God is the author and comprehends all things, it is fitting for one word to have several senses, even according to the literal sense.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for allowing multiple senses in Scripture?
options: Human readers are too confused to understand complex theology unless multiple layers of meaning are provided.
Scripture is a form of poetry, and poetry by definition relies on metaphor rather than literal historical fact.
The Old Testament was written in a different language that naturally contained more ambiguities than modern texts.
God can signify meaning through things themselves, not just words, allowing those things to point to further truths.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that unlike other sciences where words signify things, in Scripture the things signified by words also have a signification, enabling spiritual senses based on the literal.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that multiple senses cause confusion and destroy argument?
options: He argues that the senses are not multiplied by one word meaning many things, but by the things signified serving as types of others.
He admits that confusion is possible but claims that faith allows believers to ignore logical inconsistencies in the text.
He states that the objection is invalid because Holy Writ is not meant to be used for logical argumentation anyway.
He replies that God intentionally creates confusion to test the faith of those who read the Scriptures deeply.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that the multiplicity of senses does not cause equivocation because the senses arise from the things signified being types of other things, not from the words themselves being ambiguous.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the statement 'God exists' is self-evident?
options: It is self-evident in its own nature, but not self-evident to human beings.
It is self-evident only to religious experts, while remaining hidden from others.
It is completely self-evident to everyone because God is the source of all truth.
It is not self-evident in any way and requires complex proof for all people.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the proposition is self-evident in itself (because God's essence is existence), it is not self-evident to us because we do not know God's essence.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas claim the proposition 'God exists' is not self-evident to us?
options: Because humans lack knowledge of God's essential nature.
Because God's existence is hidden by the complexity of the universe.
Because truth itself is not self-evident to the human mind.
Because the concept of God is too vague for logical demonstration.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that a proposition is self-evident to us only if we know the essence of the subject and predicate; since we do not know God's essence, it is not self-evident to us.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the existence of truth is self-evident?
options: God is truth, so the existence of God is self-evident in the same way.
Truth does not exist, so the objection is based on a false premise.
The existence of truth is self-evident only to those who have studied philosophy.
The existence of truth in general is self-evident, but the existence of a Primal Truth is not.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas distinguishes between the general existence of truth, which is self-evident, and the existence of a Primal Truth (God), which is not self-evident to us.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the possibility of proving God's existence?
options: It is impossible to prove because finite effects do not match an infinite cause.
It can be demonstrated from effects that are known to us.
It cannot be demonstrated because it is an article of faith.
It can only be known through direct experience of God's essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while God's existence is not self-evident to us, it can be demonstrated from His effects, which are better known to us than He is.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why we can demonstrate God's existence?
options: God's essence is fully known to human reason, allowing for direct proof.
Every effect depends on its cause, so the effect's existence proves the cause exists.
The effects of God are proportionate to His infinite nature, making proof easy.
Faith requires scientific demonstration to be valid, so reason must confirm it.
questions.explanation: He states that since every effect depends on its cause, if the effect exists, the cause must pre-exist, allowing us to infer the cause from the known effect.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God's existence cannot be demonstrated because it is an article of faith?
options: He argues that faith is a type of scientific knowledge that produces certainty.
He claims that what is of faith can also be demonstrated by natural reason.
He states that the existence of God is self-evident and therefore not of faith.
He says such truths are preambles to faith, not articles of faith themselves.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that truths knowable by natural reason are preambles to faith, not articles of faith, and thus can be demonstrated.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the question of whether God exists?
options: It is impossible to know whether God exists or not.
God's existence is a matter of faith that cannot be logically proven.
God exists, and this can be demonstrated through five distinct arguments.
God does not exist because evil is present in the world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the existence of God can be proved in five ways, directly answering the article's question in the affirmative.

questions.q: In his first argument, why does Aquinas claim there must be a 'first mover'?
options: Because an infinite chain of movers moving other movers is impossible without a starting point.
Because God is defined as the only thing that can move itself without help.
Because everything in the world is moving, so there must be a central engine.
Because motion is an illusion created by our senses, requiring a divine explanation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if every mover were moved by another, the chain would go back infinitely, meaning there would be no first mover and thus no subsequent motion at all.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God cannot exist because evil exists?
options: The presence of evil proves that God is not all-powerful.
Evil is not real, so it does not contradict God's goodness.
God is not responsible for evil, which comes from human free will alone.
God allows evil to exist because He can bring good out of it.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas cites Augustine to say that God's infinite goodness allows evil to exist so that He may produce good from it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the question of whether God is a body?
options: God is not a body, and this truth is absolutely certain.
God is a body because Scripture describes Him with physical dimensions.
God is neither a body nor a spirit, but a unique third category.
God is a body, but only in a spiritual or metaphorical sense.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that it is 'absolutely true that God is not a body,' rejecting the idea that He has physical form.

questions.q: Which of the following is a main reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot be a body?
options: Bodies are divisible, which implies potentiality, but God is pure actuality.
Bodies are always in motion, but God is the unmoved First Mover.
Bodies have parts, but God is simple and has no internal structure.
Bodies are inanimate, and God is the most noble animate being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that bodies are divisible (and thus in potentiality), whereas God, as the First Being, must be entirely in act with no potentiality.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain the biblical phrase that God has 'eyes'?
options: It means God literally possesses physical eyes to see the world.
It suggests that God sees only what is visible to human eyes.
It is a metaphor for God's intellectual power to know things.
It indicates that God is a body with corporeal sensory organs.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the objection about corporeal parts, Aquinas states that 'eyes' attributed to God signify His power of seeing intellectually, not sensibly.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is made of matter and form?
options: God is composed of matter and form, but in a way that is unique to Him.
God is not composed of matter and form; He is pure form without any matter.
God has a soul, which means He must be a composite of matter and form.
It is impossible to know if God has matter, so we should remain silent on the issue.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states it is impossible for matter to exist in God because God is pure act and the first efficient cause, making Him essentially form alone.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot contain matter?
options: Matter is always evil, and God is perfectly good and free from evil.
Scripture never mentions God having a physical body or material parts.
Matter represents potentiality, but God is pure actuality with no potentiality.
Matter is too heavy and dense for a spiritual being like God to possess.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that matter is in potentiality, whereas God is pure act; since God has no potentiality, He cannot have matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain the biblical reference to God having a 'soul' (Objection 1)?
options: The word 'soul' in Hebrews is a mistranslation of the original Greek text.
God has a soul metaphorically, because His acts resemble the acts of a human soul.
God's soul is distinct from His essence, unlike human souls which are forms.
God has a literal soul, which serves as the form of His divine body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that a soul is attributed to God only because His acts resemble those of a soul, such as willing what is pleasing.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether God is the same as His essence or nature?
options: God’s nature is only a potential aspect of His essence.
God’s essence is a part of His nature but not identical.
God is identical with His essence or nature.
God is not identical with His essence or nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is the same as His essence or nature.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say God is identical with His essence?
options: Because God’s essence is the only thing that exists.
Because God’s essence is a composite of many parts.
Because God is simple, not made of matter and form.
Because God’s nature is always changing.
questions.explanation: He argues that since God is not composed of matter and form, the form (essence) subsists by itself, making God identical with His essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1, that God is not the same as His essence?
options: He says we can only speak of God using concrete nouns, not abstract ones.
He says the objection is based on a misunderstanding of simplicity.
He says God’s essence is a separate entity from His existence.
He says God’s essence is unknowable and therefore not identical.
questions.explanation: His reply is that we speak of God with concrete nouns for subsistence and abstract nouns for simplicity, implying God is identical with His essence.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between essence and existence in God?
options: Existence exists but not essence in God.
Essence and existence are the same in God.
Essence exists but not existence in God.
Essence and existence are distinct in God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God is both His own essence and His own existence, so they are identical.

questions.q: What is Aquinas’s main reason for saying essence and existence are identical in God?
options: Because existence is the act of essence, so they must coincide.
Because God has no potentiality, so existence cannot be separate from essence.
Because God’s essence requires no addition, making existence unnecessary.
Because God is the first efficient cause, so nothing can cause His existence apart from Himself.
questions.explanation: He notes that God has no potentiality, so existence cannot be distinct from essence, making them identical.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1 that essence and existence are not the same in God?
options: He accepts the objection and concedes essence and existence differ.
He says a thing with nothing added can still have an essence that allows addition.
He claims that God’s essence must be added by an external agent.
He argues that a thing with no addition can be of two kinds, one where essence precludes addition.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that a thing with nothing added can be either of two kinds, one where its essence precludes addition, addressing the objection.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God belongs to a category (genus)?
options: God is a principle that can be reduced to the category of quantity.
God is not contained in any category, whether as a member or a principle.
God is contained in the category of substance because He exists independently.
God is a specific type of being that fits under the general category of existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is not in a genus in either way: not as a species contained under it, and not as a principle reducible to it.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot be a specific type within a general category?
options: God lacks the sensory nature required to be defined by a genus and difference.
God is too perfect to be measured by any other standard or comparison.
God is the measure of all things, which prevents Him from being measured by a genus.
God’s existence is identical to His essence, whereas categories require a distinction between them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in any genus, existence and essence differ, but in God, existence is His essence, making it impossible for Him to be a species of a genus.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God is the measure of all substances, implying He is in the genus of substance?
options: He claims that substance is not a valid category, so the objection is based on a false premise.
He states that God measures substances only through His effects, not through His own essence.
He argues that God is not a proportionate measure, but that things have being by resembling Him.
He agrees that God is a proportionate measure, so He must share the genus of substance.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that God is not a 'proportionate measure' (homogeneous with the measured), but rather the standard by which all things have being through resemblance.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the presence of accidental properties in God?
options: God has no accidents because He exists outside of all genera.
God possesses certain essential accidents that define His nature.
God has accidents, but they are different from those in created things.
God has no accidents because He is pure actuality without potentiality.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that there can be no accident in God, primarily because a subject is related to its accidents as potentiality to actuality, and God has no potentiality.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is it impossible for God to have any accidental properties?
options: Because substance is prior to accidents, so God must be pure substance.
Because accidents require a subject that has potentiality, which God lacks.
Because God is the first cause and cannot be caused by anything else.
Because God is absolute being, and nothing can be added to absolute being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that a subject is compared to its accidents as potentiality to actuality, meaning the subject is made actual by them. Since God has no potentiality, He cannot have accidents.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that virtue and wisdom are accidents in us but must be substances in God?
options: He argues that these terms are not used in the same sense for God and us.
He agrees that these are substances in God but accidents in us.
He states that God is the first principle of all genera of accidents.
He claims that heat cannot be a substantial form in any context.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that virtue and wisdom are not predicated of God and humans univocally (in the same way), so their status as accidents in us does not imply they are substances in God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the nature of God?
options: God is completely simple, with no parts or composition of any kind.
God is simple in essence but composed of matter and form.
God is composite because He contains all the perfections of creation.
God is neither simple nor composite, but a unique third category.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly argues that God is 'nowise composite, but is altogether simple,' rejecting any mixture of parts, matter, or form.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for God's simplicity?
options: God is too powerful to be broken down into smaller components.
God chose to remain simple to distinguish Himself from humans.
God is the first being and uncaused, so He cannot be made of parts.
God is simple because He is invisible and cannot be touched.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that every composite thing has a cause and depends on its parts, but God is the first, uncaused being, so He cannot be composite.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that composite things are better than simple ones?
options: God is simple, but He creates composite beings to show His power over parts.
The objection is wrong because chemical compounds are not truly better than simple elements.
God is actually composite, but we cannot perceive His complexity due to our limited senses.
In creation, goodness is spread across many things, but in God, all perfection is united in one simple being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that while created goodness requires many things to be perfect, divine goodness is fully contained in one simple thing.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is a component part of created things?
options: God is absolutely simple and cannot be a part of any compound.
God is the material substance from which all things are made.
God is the formal shape that gives definition to all matter.
God is the soul that animates the entire universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly rejects the ideas that God is matter, soul, or form, concluding that God is the first efficient cause and thus cannot enter into the composition of anything.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot be a part of a compound?
options: Created things are too imperfect to hold the divine essence within them.
God exists only in the spiritual realm, which is separate from physical composition.
God is too powerful to be contained within the limits of physical matter.
God is the first efficient cause, and causes are not numerically identical to the parts of their effects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that as the first efficient cause, God is not identical to the form or matter of the things He causes, just as a father is not numerically identical to the form of his son.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God is the 'being of all things' and therefore a part of them?
options: He argues that Dionysius was speaking metaphorically about God's love, not His ontological status.
He says God is the being of things only as their efficient and exemplar cause, not as their essence.
He states that God's being is distinct from creation but still physically intermixed with it.
He claims that the 'being' of things is actually primary matter, not God.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that while God is called the being of all things, this refers to His role as their cause and model, not that He constitutes their essential makeup.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether God is perfect?
options: God is imperfect because existence is universal and modifiable.
God is imperfect because he is not made.
God is perfect only in his essence, not his existence.
God is perfect because he is the most actual first principle.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says the first active principle must be most actual and therefore most perfect.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God’s perfection?
options: Because existence is universal, it is the most imperfect thing.
Because God is the first principle, he is made by matter.
Because God is the first beginning, he must be imperfect like a seed.
Because God is not material, he is fully actual and cannot be made.
questions.explanation: He argues that as a non‑material first principle, God is fully actual, making him most perfect.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer Objection 1, that God cannot be perfect because he is not made?
options: He says the word “perfect” applies to things that are made, so God cannot be perfect.
He agrees that God is not made, so he is not perfect.
He says that even though God is not made, the term “perfect” can still apply to him.
He says that being not made makes God perfect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that the word ‘perfect’ can still apply to God, even though he is not made.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between goodness and being?
options: Goodness is a subset of being that can be more or less.
Goodness is a form that is never identical to being.
Goodness is a property that exists separately from being.
Goodness and being are the same in reality, differing only in idea.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that goodness and being are really the same, differing only in thought.

questions.q: What main reason does Aquinas give for saying goodness and being are the same?
options: Because being is the form of all things, and good is the form of being.
Because good is what all desire, and desire only applies to actual things.
Because goodness can be more or less, just like being.
Because everything that exists is perfect, and perfection is what makes things good.
questions.explanation: He argues that goodness is what is desirable, and desire applies to perfection, which is actual existence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1 that goodness and being differ in thought?
options: He agrees that they differ in thought and therefore must be different in reality.
He denies the objection by saying that thought cannot distinguish between being and goodness.
He says they are the same in reality but differ in thought, so they are not predicated absolutely the same way.
He claims that being is a form of goodness, so they are identical.
questions.explanation: His reply states that although they are the same really, they differ in thought and thus are not predicated absolutely the same way.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between being and goodness?
options: Goodness is prior because it represents the ultimate goal of all actions.
Being and goodness are identical concepts with no order of priority.
Being comes before goodness because it is the first thing the mind grasps.
Goodness comes before being because it applies to more things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'in idea being is prior to goodness' because being is the first thing conceived by the intellect.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that being is understood before goodness?
options: Because goodness is a more universal concept that covers non-existent things.
Because all other desirable qualities are specific types of being.
Because the intellect can only know things that actually exist in reality.
Because Dionysius listed goodness first among the names of God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that everything is knowable only inasmuch as it is in actuality, making being the primary object of the intellect.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that non-existence can be desirable (e.g., Judas not being born)?
options: By arguing that non-existence is desirable only because it removes an evil that lacks being.
By stating that non-existence is a form of potential being that is actually preferred.
By claiming that Judas’s case is an exception to the rule that being is good.
By suggesting that the desire for non-existence proves goodness is more universal.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas says non-being is desirable only relatively, specifically insofar as it removes an evil that deprives a thing of being.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between existence and goodness?
options: Goodness is an extra quality added to being, not inherent in existence itself.
Every existing thing is good simply by virtue of the fact that it exists.
Some things are evil in their very nature, so not all beings are good.
Only physical substances are good, while abstract concepts lack moral value.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'every being, as being, is good,' rejecting the idea that goodness is merely added or that some beings are inherently evil.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is every existing thing considered good?
options: Because God commanded that all existing things must be regarded as morally good.
Because existence is a measurable quantity that can be weighed against non-existence.
Because all existing things possess the specific virtue of kindness toward others.
Because existence implies a state of actuality and perfection, which makes it desirable.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that being implies actuality and perfection, and perfection implies desirability, which is the definition of goodness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that evil things exist, so not all beings are good?
options: He claims that evil is a separate substance that exists alongside good things.
He suggests that evil things are actually good but are misunderstood by humans.
He states that evil is a type of being that lacks the quality of goodness.
He argues that evil is not a positive thing but a lack or deficiency of being.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that nothing is evil 'formally as being,' but only insofar as it lacks being or perfection.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between goodness and the end of an action?
options: Goodness acts as an efficient cause that creates things from nothing.
Goodness is primarily a formal cause that defines what a thing is.
Goodness is identical to beauty and therefore has no causal aspect.
Goodness has the aspect of a final cause because all things desire it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that since goodness is what all things desire, it has the aspect of an end (final cause).

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why goodness implies the aspect of an end?
options: Because goodness is self-diffusive and gives existence to all things.
Because goodness is praised as beauty, which relates to form.
Because God's goodness is the efficient cause of our existence.
Because goodness is the object of desire, which characterizes an end.
questions.explanation: The text argues that goodness implies the aspect of an end specifically because it is that which all things desire.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that goodness is an efficient cause because it is 'self-diffusive'?
options: He argues that self-diffusiveness describes how an end moves the agent to act.
He states that only God is self-diffusive, while other things are not.
He agrees that goodness is an efficient cause but denies it is self-diffusive.
He claims that self-diffusiveness is a property of beauty, not goodness.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that goodness is described as self-diffusive in the sense that an end moves the agent.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the essence of goodness consists in mode, species, and order?
options: No, because these three concepts are themselves good and would require an infinite chain of further qualities.
Yes, but only for physical objects that possess weight, number, and measure in a literal sense.
Yes, because goodness is perfection, which requires proper measure, specific form, and right direction.
No, because mode, species, and order belong only to being, not to the distinct concept of goodness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that goodness is perfection. Perfection implies having the right measure (mode), the correct form (species), and the proper tendency toward an end (order).

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for linking goodness to mode, species, and order?
options: Scripture explicitly states that all things are ordered by measure, number, and weight, which defines moral value.
Goodness is defined as perfection, and a thing is perfect only when it has its proper form and lacks nothing.
These three qualities are caused by weight, number, and measure, which are the fundamental sources of all good.
Evil is merely the absence of these three qualities, so their presence must automatically constitute goodness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that everything is good insofar as it is perfect. A thing is perfect if it lacks nothing according to its nature, which involves its mode, species, and order.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that we can speak of an 'evil mode' or 'evil order'?
options: He agrees that evil modes exist, proving that the essence of goodness cannot consist in these three things.
He claims that evil modes are actually good in a hidden way that humans fail to understand fully.
He argues that mode, species, and order are purely physical concepts that cannot apply to moral evil.
He says such terms are used loosely to describe a deficiency or a mismatch with what is proper.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that an 'evil mode' is called so only because it is less than it ought to be or does not belong to what it should.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the division of goodness into the virtuous, useful, and pleasant?
options: The division is valid because it reflects how different things satisfy human desire.
The division is only valid for human goodness and does not apply to goodness in general.
The division is invalid because these categories overlap within a single category of being.
The division is invalid because the useful is merely a means to the virtuous and pleasant.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the division is right because it describes how things are desirable or serve as ends for the appetite, which applies to goodness as such.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why this three-part division works for all good things?
options: Goodness is identical to being, so it must be divided by the ten standard categories of existence.
Goodness is defined by how it stops the movement of desire, whether as a goal, a means, or a state of rest.
Goodness is analogical, meaning it is predicated chiefly of the virtuous and only secondarily of others.
Goodness is divided by opposites, and the virtuous, useful, and pleasant are the three fundamental opposites.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that everything good is desirable, and the division maps to how desire is terminated: by the end itself (virtuous), the means (useful), or the rest in the thing (pleasant).

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the useful is not distinct from the virtuous and pleasant?
options: He claims that the useful is a separate substance that exists independently of the virtuous and pleasant.
He states that goodness is applied to these three in different degrees, with the virtuous being primary.
He argues that the useful is actually the most important part of goodness because it enables the other two.
He explains that the useful is only good insofar as it leads to the virtuous or pleasant, so it is distinct.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that goodness is not the same thing in all three (univocal) but is applied analogically, with priority given to the virtuous.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the question, "Whether God is the supreme good?"
options: God is a good but not supreme because he is not comparable to other goods.
God is not the supreme good because he is simple.
God is the supreme good, simple and most excellent.
God is a compound good, not supreme.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God is the supreme good, simple and most excellent.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for calling God the supreme good?
options: Because God is the end of all things and is desired by all.
Because all desired perfections flow from Him as the first cause.
Because God is comparable to other goods within the same genus.
Because God is a compound good that adds to all other goods.
questions.explanation: He argues that all desired perfections flow from God as the first cause, making Him the supreme good.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 2, which says that "Good is what all desire" implies only God is good?
options: He denies that anything is desired, so the objection fails.
He says that only essential goodness is God, not every desired thing.
He accepts that all desired things are God, so God is supreme.
He argues that good is not what all desire, but what is desired.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that "good is what all desire" means that whatever is desired has the nature of good, not that only God is good.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding who is essentially good?
options: Every existing thing is good by its very nature.
No being is good essentially, including God.
Only God is good by His very nature.
God is good, but other things are good by accident.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God alone is good essentially, rejecting the idea that all beings share this quality by their own essence.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why only God is essentially good?
options: God is the only being that does not have any accidents or properties.
God is the only thing that exists without needing to be caused.
God alone possesses all forms of perfection fully within His own essence.
God is the only being that is desired by all other creatures.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that goodness corresponds to perfection, and only God has all three types of perfection (existence, necessary attributes, and final end) as part of His own essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'good' is interchangeable with 'being'?
options: He argues that goodness is a separate thing that is added to being.
He claims that 'one' and 'good' are completely different concepts.
He agrees that all beings are good because being is always desired.
He says creatures have being, but their essence is not being itself.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that while creatures have being, their essence is not identical to being itself, so they are not good essentially.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether all things are good by divine goodness?
options: All things are called good because they participate in God's goodness, which is the source of all goodness.
Nothing is truly good except God, so calling other things good is merely a metaphorical error.
All things are good only because God directly labels them as good, without any internal quality of their own.
Each thing is good by its own standard, completely independent of any connection to God's goodness.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that everything is called good from divine goodness as the first principle, participating in it through assimilation.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why things are called good by divine goodness?
options: Augustine argued that God is the only true good, making all other goods illusory.
Boethius stated that goodness is defined solely by how much a thing resembles God physically.
God is the first being and good essentially, and other things share in this nature imperfectly.
Plato's theory of separate ideas proves that goodness exists independently of physical things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God is essentially being and good, and other things are good by participating in this primary goodness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that things are good by their own goodness, not God's?
options: He rejects the idea that things have any goodness, saying only God possesses the quality of good.
He claims that Augustine was wrong to suggest that God is the good of every good.
He argues that while things have their own formal goodness, it is a likeness of divine goodness.
He states that individual things have no goodness of their own, only borrowed labels from God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that each thing is good by its own goodness, which is formally its own but derived from the similitude of divine goodness.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is infinite?
options: God is infinite in the sense of being an endless physical body.
God is infinite because His being is not limited by anything else.
God is finite because He is a specific thing and not another.
God is not infinite because He is the most perfect being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that God is infinite and perfect because His being is self-subsisting and not received in or limited by any other thing.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God's infinity is a sign of perfection?
options: Because God is a form that has not yet been given a specific shape.
Because God flows forth infinitely from the first principle of nature.
Because God's being is not determined or restricted by any other reality.
Because God has no physical parts or matter to limit His size.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while matter is imperfect when infinite, form is perfect when not contracted by matter; since God is pure being not received in anything, He is perfectly infinite.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God cannot be infinite because He is not a body with quantity?
options: He argues that quantity is a form of matter, which does not apply to God.
He claims that God is actually a body, but an invisible one.
He states that quantity is the only way to measure divine perfection.
He says that God is infinite in quantity, just like the ancient philosophers thought.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that quantity is terminated by form and relates to matter, so this type of infinity cannot be attributed to God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of an actually infinite multitude?
options: It is possible only if the things involved are not opposed to each other.
It is possible because potentiality can always be made actual.
It is impossible for an actually infinite multitude to exist in any form.
It is possible if the infinity is accidental rather than absolute.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is impossible for an actually infinite multitude to exist, whether absolute or accidental, because every created multitude must be numbered.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for rejecting the existence of an actually infinite multitude?
options: Every created thing falls under a specific number intended by the Creator.
It is impossible to pass through an infinite medium to reach existence.
An infinite number of causes would prevent any work from ever being finished.
The species of geometric figures are infinite, which contradicts physical reality.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because every created thing is comprehended under a clear intention of the Creator, it must be contained within a certain number, making an actual infinite impossible.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that number can be multiplied to infinity?
options: The objection is valid, but only applies to potential, not actual, infinity.
Infinite multitude is actualized successively over time, not all at once.
Infinity exists in the division of magnitude, not in the addition of number.
Number cannot be multiplied to infinity because matter is finite.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that while number can increase to infinity, this happens successively (one after another), not all at once as an actual existing whole.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding God's presence in the world?
options: God is present in every existing thing as the cause of its being.
God is only present in things that are good and free from sin.
God is above all things and therefore not contained within them.
God is present in things only at the moment they first come into existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is in all things as the cause of their being, rejecting the idea that He is only above or only in good things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God being in all things?
options: God is the most powerful agent, so He must touch everything.
God is contained by things just as a soul contains a body.
God must be joined to things immediately to preserve their existence.
God is physically located inside every object in the universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because God preserves things in being, He must be joined to them immediately, similar to how a mover touches what it moves.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God is not in demons because light and darkness have no fellowship?
options: He argues that demons are actually good beings that are misunderstood.
He claims that demons do not exist, so the objection is irrelevant.
He agrees that God is not in demons because they are evil.
He says God is in demons only insofar as they have being, not in their sin.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas clarifies that God is in demons only regarding their nature as beings, not regarding the deformity of their sin.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is everywhere by essence, presence, and power?
options: God is absent from physical matter, existing only within the minds of those who know and love Him.
God is in all things by power, presence, and essence, each describing a different aspect of His relationship to creation.
God is only in things by His power, because He created them but does not sustain their existence directly.
God is in things only by His essence, meaning He is the fundamental substance of every created object.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that God is in all things by His power (as ruler), by His presence (as observer), and by His essence (as the cause of their being).

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is God said to be in all things by His 'essence'?
options: Because He shares the same essential nature as all created things, making Him part of them.
Because He is physically located inside every object, making up its material structure.
Because His own substance is present to all things as the direct cause of their existence.
Because His essence is defined by the sum total of all things that exist in the universe.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that God is in things by His essence not because He is part of their essence, but because His substance is present to them as the cause of their being.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God should be in things by His knowledge and will, just as by His power?
options: He argues that knowledge and will imply the object is in God, not that God is in the object.
He agrees that God is in things by knowledge, but says power is a separate, unrelated concept.
He claims that God's knowledge is limited to spiritual beings, not physical objects or powers.
He states that knowledge and will are less powerful than physical force, so they do not apply.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that knowledge and will require the thing known or willed to be in the knower/willer, so things are more truly in God than God is in them by these modes.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding who is everywhere?
options: The universe is everywhere because there is no physical space outside of it.
Only God is everywhere in His entire self, regardless of any new places that might exist.
Primary matter is everywhere because it exists within all physical bodies.
The soul is everywhere because it can see and feel in different parts of the body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while other things may be present in various places, only God is present in His whole self in every place, no matter how many places are imagined.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why this belongs to God alone?
options: God is the universal concept that applies to all things simultaneously.
God must be in every place because nothing can exist without Him.
God is the number that constitutes the whole universe.
God is an infinite body that fills all available space completely.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God must be in all places because nothing can exist except by Him, making His presence necessary in any possible location.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the universe is everywhere because nothing exists outside it?
options: He argues that the universe is only in one specific place, not everywhere.
He agrees that the universe is everywhere because it contains all possible places.
He claims the universe is everywhere only if it is considered an infinite body.
He says the universe is not everywhere because it would not exist in new, hypothetical places.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the universe is not 'absolutely' everywhere because if other places existed beyond it, the universe would not be in them.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about God's immutability?
options: God is completely immutable, never changing.
God changes only in moral actions.
God can change in ways that are not visible.
God's immutability is conditional on time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states God is altogether immutable, without any potentiality or change.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God's immutability?
options: God's immutability is a result of His simple nature.
God's immutability follows from His eternal nature alone.
God cannot move because He is not subject to space.
God is pure act, lacking any potentiality that could allow change.
questions.explanation: He argues that because God is pure act with no potentiality, nothing can change Him.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 2 about Wisdom being mobile?
options: He says Wisdom is mobile only figuratively, not literally.
He agrees Wisdom is mobile and so God is mobile too.
He says Wisdom's mobility is a metaphor for divine influence.
He claims Wisdom is immobile, contradicting Scripture.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that Wisdom is called mobile by similitude, not literally, so God remains immutable.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether immutability belongs to God alone?
options: God is unchangeable, but blessed souls in heaven are also fully immutable.
Nothing is truly immutable because all things are subject to time.
Only God is completely unchangeable; every creature is changeable in some way.
God and angels are both completely unchangeable because they lack matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'God alone is altogether immutable; whereas every creature is in some way mutable,' rejecting the idea that any creature shares God's absolute immutability.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why every creature is mutable?
options: Creatures depend on God's power for their existence and preservation.
Creatures constantly change their location in the physical universe.
All creatures are made of matter which is inherently unstable.
God intentionally created creatures to be imperfect and changing.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creatures are mutable because their existence depends entirely on God's will to preserve them; if God withdrew this action, they would cease to exist.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas address the claim that blessed angels are immutable?
options: He claims that blessed angels are completely immutable in every single way.
He argues that angels are not actually blessed until they become human.
He agrees they are immutable in being but notes they can change place.
He states that angels do not exist in heaven but in a different realm.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that while good angels have immutability of being and election, 'there remains in them mutability as regards place,' meaning they can still move.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the definition of eternity?
options: The definition is wrong because eternity should be defined using 'existence' instead of 'life'.
The definition is valid because it correctly describes eternity's lack of succession and limits.
The definition is flawed because it uses negative terms like 'interminable'.
The definition is inaccurate because eternity is simple and cannot be described as 'whole'.
questions.explanation: Aquinas accepts the definition, explaining that 'interminable' refers to having no beginning or end, and 'simultaneously whole' refers to the lack of succession.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for understanding eternity in this way?
options: The definition relies on the fact that God possesses multiple days and times simultaneously.
We understand simple, unchanging things by contrasting them with the time we experience in movement.
Eternity is a type of duration that measures the existence of all living creatures.
It is necessary to use negative language because eternity is a defective form of being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since we know simple things through compound ones, we grasp eternity (which has no before or after) by contrasting it with time (which is the measure of movement).

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'whole' implies having parts, which eternity lacks?
options: He states that eternity has parts, but they are invisible to human understanding.
He suggests that 'whole' is a metaphor for God's physical body, which has parts.
He argues that 'whole' means lacking nothing, not that it is composed of distinct parts.
He agrees that 'whole' is an improper term because eternity is fundamentally simple.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that eternity is called 'whole' because it is lacking in nothing, not because it is made up of parts.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is eternal?
options: God is eternal because He is completely unchanged and is His own existence.
God is eternal because He is the very source of time.
God is eternal only in the sense that He lasts for a very long time.
God is not eternal because He exists outside of all measurement.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because God is supremely immutable (unchanging), He is supremely eternal, and He is not just eternal but is eternity itself.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God being eternal?
options: God is eternal because He is before and after all other forms of duration.
Eternity is a necessary attribute for any being that creates the universe.
God is eternal because He is supremely immutable, unlike changing creatures.
God is eternal because He is the author of the concept of time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the idea of eternity follows from immutability, just as time follows from movement; since God is supremely immutable, He is supremely eternal.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God cannot be measured by eternity?
options: The idea of measurement applies only to our minds, not to God Himself.
Eternity measures God in the same way that time measures human life.
God is not measured because He exists outside the concept of eternity.
God is measured by eternity because He is the standard for all time.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that the notion of measurement is a feature of our apprehension, not a property that applies to God.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who truly possesses eternity in the strictest sense?
options: All necessary truths, because they exist eternally in the divine mind.
The earth and hills, because Scripture describes them as standing forever.
God alone, because He is the only being that is completely unchanging.
Angels and the blessed, because they enjoy unchanging vision of God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that true eternity follows from immutability, and since God alone is altogether immutable, eternity properly belongs to Him alone.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for God being the only truly eternal being?
options: Necessary truths are only eternal because they reside in God's mind.
Scripture explicitly states that God is the only one who lives forever.
Other beings are corruptible, whereas God is made of divine substance.
Eternity requires total immutability, and only God is entirely unchanging.
questions.explanation: Aquinas links eternity directly to immutability, stating that because God alone is completely immutable, He alone is truly eternal.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that hellfire is eternal, implying God is not the only eternal thing?
options: Hellfire is called eternal only because its duration never ends, though it involves change.
The fire of hell shares in God's eternity by participating in divine immutability.
Hellfire is a metaphor for spiritual pain and does not literally exist in time.
Scripture uses 'eternal' loosely for hell, but strictly for God's nature.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that hellfire is termed eternal solely due to its endless duration, not because it is immutable like God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether there is only one aeviternity?
options: There is no single measure because spiritual and physical things differ too much.
There is only one aeviternity, shared by all changeless beings.
Aeviternity does not exist because all things are either temporal or eternal.
There are many aeviternities, one for each angel or heavenly body.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as there is one time for all temporal things, there is one aeviternity for all changeless things, measured by the first such being.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why aeviternity is one?
options: The number of things measured determines the unity of the measure itself.
God created all spiritual and heavenly substances at the exact same moment.
All changeless things share a single, simple measure derived from the first such being.
Primary matter serves as the common subject for all durations and measures.
questions.explanation: He states that unity comes from the 'first movement' or principle which is most simple, serving as the single measure for all other durations in that category.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that different types of beings (like angels and stars) should have different measures?
options: He claims that angels and stars are actually the same type of substance.
He admits the objection is correct and that there are indeed different measures.
He argues they differ in nature but share the same changeless existence, requiring one measure.
He says that only spiritual beings have aeviternity, while stars have time.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that despite differing in genus, heavenly bodies and spirits agree in having changeless being, so they are measured by the same aeviternity.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between "one" and "being"?
options: "One" does not add any reality to "being" but simply means it is undivided.
"One" and "being" have completely different meanings and refer to separate things.
"One" is an addition to "being" because it divides the concept of existence.
"One" adds a new reality to "being" by making it a specific type of quantity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that "one" does not add any reality to "being" but is only a negation of division, meaning it signifies undivided being.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why "one" does not add reality to "being"?
options: Because calling something "one" is redundant and adds no new information.
Because simple things are always divided while compound things are undivided.
Because every existing thing must be undivided in order to possess its being.
Because number is a species of quantity that must be distinct from being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the being of anything consists in undivision; therefore, "one" (undivided) is the same as "being" and adds no new reality.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that saying "being is one" is redundant?
options: He claims that "being" is always divided, so "one" is a necessary correction.
He rejects the objection by stating that "one" and "being" are contradictory terms.
He agrees that it is redundant because the words have exactly the same meaning.
He argues that "one" adds a new idea to "being" even if it adds no reality.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas says it is not redundant because "one" adds an idea to "being," even though it does not add reality.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is one?
options: God is one because His nature cannot be shared by others.
God is one only in the way that numbers are one.
God is not one because perfection requires multiple beings.
God is not one because the Bible mentions many gods.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God is one because He is simple; His specific nature is not communicable to many, unlike human traits which can be shared.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why there cannot be many gods?
options: Multiple gods would fail to agree on how to order the universe.
God's simplicity means His nature is unique and cannot be replicated.
The concept of 'one' is too imperfect to apply to God.
The world's harmony proves that only one deity exists.
questions.explanation: While he offers three proofs, the first and foundational one is that God is simple, meaning He is identical to His own nature, which cannot be shared by multiple entities.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the Bible mentions many gods?
options: He argues that planets are actually angels, not gods.
He claims the term 'gods' refers to human rulers only.
He explains that 'many gods' reflects the error of idolaters.
He says the Bible is wrong about the number of gods.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that the mention of many gods arises from the error of those who mistakenly worshipped stars and parts of the world.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is supremely one?
options: God is one, but unity is a potentiality in Him.
God is one only in a metaphorical sense.
God is one in the highest possible degree.
God is one, but not more so than other beings.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that because God is supremely being and supremely undivided, it is manifest that God is 'one' in the supreme degree.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God being supremely one?
options: God is the only being that lacks any division, actual or potential.
God is one because He is the cause of all other numbers.
God is one because He is essentially good and therefore undivided.
God is one because He is simpler than a geometric point.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that to be supremely one is to be supremely being and supremely undivided; God fits this because He is absolutely simple and divided neither actually nor potentially.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a point or mathematical unity is more indivisible (and thus more one) than God?
options: He states that points and mathematical unity are not considered beings in the same way God is.
He asserts that God is more indivisible because He is infinite in size.
He argues that points and mathematical unity are not supremely being because they exist only within a subject.
He claims that points and mathematical unity are actually divisible in some ways.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that a point and mathematical unity are not supremely one because they have being only in some subject, unlike God who is being itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion about how the created intellect sees God's essence?
options: It sees God through a perfect copy of His existence.
It sees God through a created image that acts as a mirror.
It sees God directly, without any created image representing Him.
It sees God only through the likeness of physical objects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that no created likeness can represent God's essence because God is existence itself and contains all perfections, so the essence must be united to the seer directly.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why a created image cannot show God's essence?
options: God's essence is His own existence, which no created thing can be.
Human eyes are too weak to handle the brightness of God.
God is too far away for human minds to grasp clearly.
Created images are always distorted by the viewer's biases.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that God's essence is identical to His existence, whereas every created form is distinct from its existence, making a created likeness impossible.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that Augustine said a likeness of God is made in us?
options: He says Augustine meant the likeness is in God, not us.
He says Augustine was wrong about all knowledge of God.
He says Augustine meant this happens only in earthly life.
He says Augustine was referring to physical resemblance only.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that Augustine was speaking about our knowledge of God while we are here on earth, not the final vision.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can be seen with the physical eye?
options: God can be seen by the physical eye after the resurrection of the body.
God can be seen through a vision of the imagination, like in biblical dreams.
God can be seen by the physical eye if the eyes are glorified and strengthened.
God cannot be seen by the physical eye or imagination, but only by the intellect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is incorporeal and therefore cannot be seen by any sense or imagination, which are tied to physical organs, but only by the intellect.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the physical eye cannot see God?
options: The human eye is too weak to handle the brightness of God's presence.
God chooses to remain hidden from physical sight to test human faith.
Physical senses are limited to seeing material things, while God is non-material.
The physical eye can only see things that are close by, and God is too distant.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because sight is an act of a physical organ, it is proportional to physical nature and cannot go beyond corporeal things to see an incorporeal God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that Job saw God with his physical eye?
options: He argues that Job was actually seeing a physical representation of God.
He explains that Job's 'eye' refers to the mind's eye, not the physical organ.
He says that Job's statement was metaphorical and not meant to be taken literally at all.
He claims that Job's eyes were miraculously changed to see spiritual things.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the phrase 'my eye seeth Thee' should be understood as referring to the 'mind's eye' or intellectual vision, not the fleshly eye.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the ability of a created mind to see God's essence?
options: A created mind cannot see God's essence without God's grace helping it.
No created mind can ever see God's essence, even with divine help.
A created mind can see God's essence using only its own natural abilities.
Angels can see God's essence naturally, but human beings cannot at all.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that it is impossible for any created intellect to see the Divine essence by its own natural power; it requires God to unite Himself to the intellect by grace.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why a created mind cannot naturally see God's essence?
options: Created minds are too weak and defective to handle the brightness of God.
God is too far away from the physical world for minds to reach Him.
God's mode of being is self-existent, which exceeds the nature of any creature.
