questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the presence of will in God?
options: God lacks a will because He has no external goals to pursue.
God has a will only to move other things into action.
God has no will because desire implies a lack of perfection.
God has a will because it follows from having an intellect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that will follows intellect, and since God has intellect, He must also have will.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for believing God has a will?
options: Will is a natural consequence of having an intellect in any being.
God requires a will to be moved by external causes.
Will is necessary for God to define His own essence.
God needs a will to seek out goods He does not yet possess.
questions.explanation: He states that just as animal appetite exists in sensible beings, will exists in intellectual beings because it follows upon intellect.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God cannot be moved because He is unmoved?
options: He says that God’s will is separate from His essence to avoid motion.
He states that God is not moved at all, so the objection stands.
He claims that God is moved by the desires of created beings.
He argues that God is moved by His own essence, which is His goodness.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that God's will is His essence, so it is moved by itself alone, not by another.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God wills things other than Himself?
options: God does not will other things because His will is identical to His existence.
God wills only Himself because His own goodness is completely sufficient for Him.
God wills both Himself and other things, with Himself as the ultimate goal.
God wills other things primarily to increase His own perfection and power.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God wills both Himself and other things apart from Himself, positioning Himself as the end and other things as ordered to that end.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God wills other things to exist?
options: Perfect beings naturally share their goodness with others, and God is the most perfect being.
Other things move God's will, which is necessary for divine action to occur.
God wills other things because He lacks the ability to exist solely by Himself.
God needs other things to complete His own nature and avoid isolation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that it is the nature of the will, especially the perfect divine will, to communicate its possessed good to others, just as perfect natural things spread their good.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God's will cannot be moved by anything other than Himself?
options: He claims that other things move God's will directly, just as they move human appetites.
He says the end (God's goodness) is what moves the will, so no external movement is needed.
He argues that God's will is not moved at all, so the objection is irrelevant.
He states that God's will is manifold, allowing it to be moved by multiple external sources.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that when we will something for an end, it is the end itself that moves the will, not the intermediate means or external objects.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether God’s will causes things?
options: God’s will is irrelevant to creation.
God’s will causes only natural beings.
God’s will is the cause of all things.
God’s nature, not will, causes things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the will of God is the cause of things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for this conclusion?
options: God’s will is the only cause of natural agents.
God’s intellect alone determines all effects.
God’s nature is undetermined, so he must act by will.
God acts by intellect and will, not by necessity of nature.
questions.explanation: He argues that because God is first and acts by intellect and will, his will causes effects.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1 about Dionysius’ statement?
options: He says Dionysius means God’s goodness is given to all, not just some.
He says Dionysius’ statement is irrelevant to the question.
He says Dionysius excludes election entirely.
He says Dionysius’ view is correct and he accepts it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that Dionysius does not exclude election absolutely, only that God’s goodness is communicated to all, not just some.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the cause of God's will?
options: God's will is caused by the need to create order in the universe.
No cause can be assigned to the divine will.
God's will is caused by His desire to avoid irrational actions.
God's will is caused by His intellect understanding the good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'In no wise has the will of God a cause,' rejecting the idea that any external or internal factor compels His will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God's will has no cause?
options: God's intellect is separate from His will, preventing any causal link.
God acts freely to ensure that secondary causes remain effective.
God wills all things in a single act, so nothing can cause itself.
God is perfect and therefore does not need reasons to act.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because God understands and wills everything in one single act, the end cannot be the cause of the means, since a thing cannot be its own cause.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God might act irrationally if His will has no cause?
options: He argues that God's will is the cause of all rationality in the world.
He agrees that God acts without reason to show His absolute power.
He claims that irrationality is impossible for any being, including God.
He says God's will is reasonable because He orders means to ends.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that God's will is reasonable not because something causes it, but because He wills one thing to be for the sake of another.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God's will is always fulfilled?
options: God's will is sometimes frustrated by the free choices of sinful humans.
God's will is always fulfilled because it is the universal cause that includes all other causes.
God's will is fulfilled only in the spiritual realm, but not always in physical events.
God's will is not always fulfilled when secondary causes, like human weakness, interfere.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God's will is the universal cause of all things, meaning no effect can escape its order, so it must always be fulfilled.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God's will cannot fail to produce its effect?
options: Because the universe is designed so that secondary causes never actually hinder the first cause.
Because God only wills things that are already guaranteed to happen without any resistance.
Because God's will is the universal cause, any particular failure is still part of its overall order.
Because God is all-powerful and can simply override any secondary causes that try to block Him.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that while a particular cause might fail due to a hindrance, that hindrance is itself included in the order of the universal cause (God).

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God wills all good, but not all good exists?
options: The objection is wrong because all good that could exist actually does exist in the world.
God wills all possible good virtually within Himself, but not all of it exists in created things.
God does not will all good; He only wills the good that He chooses to create.
God's will is limited by the nature of created things, so He cannot will all good.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that all being and truth exist virtually in God, even if they do not all exist in created things.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the will of God?
options: It is changeable because God can choose to stop doing things.
It is entirely unchangeable and remains permanently the same.
It changes locally when God moves from one action to another.
It changes when God decides to alter His plans for humanity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that the will of God is entirely unchangeable, rejecting the idea that it shifts or varies.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God's will cannot change?
options: God's will is distinct from His actions, so actions can change without it.
God's knowledge and substance are unchangeable, so His will must be too.
God is too powerful to allow His intentions to be altered by events.
God only wills things that are necessary, preventing any possibility of change.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that a change in will requires a change in knowledge or substance; since God's knowledge and substance are unchangeable, His will is also unchangeable.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God 'repents' of making man?
options: He says the phrase is metaphorical, describing how we perceive divine action.
He claims that repentance is a necessary part of God's voluntary nature.
He states that God never made man, so there is nothing to repent of.
He argues that God actually changed His mind after seeing human sin.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that the language of repentance is metaphorical and based on the likeness of our nature, not a literal change in God's will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether God's will makes the things He wills happen necessarily?
options: God's will never imposes necessity; all created things are purely accidental.
God's will imposes necessity on some things, but contingency on others.
God's will makes everything happen necessarily, without exception.
Necessity depends entirely on secondary causes, independent of God's will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the divine will imposes necessity on some things willed but not on all, depending on how God intends them to occur.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the primary reason why some effects of God's will are contingent rather than necessary?
options: God specifically wills that certain things happen contingently for the good order of the universe.
God lacks the power to make every single event happen with absolute necessity.
Secondary causes are inherently weak and often fail to execute God's plan.
The nature of created matter prevents any effect from being strictly necessary.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that effects are contingent not because secondary causes are defective, but because God wills them to be so and prepares contingent causes accordingly.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that if God wills something, it must happen with absolute necessity?
options: He asserts that human free will completely overrides God's will in matters of salvation.
He argues that the necessity is conditional: if God wills it, it happens, but not always absolutely.
He states that God's will changes over time, allowing for different outcomes in different eras.
He claims Augustine was mistaken and that God's will can be hindered by secondary causes.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas explains that the necessity is conditional (if God wills, it must be) rather than absolute in all cases.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the five expressions of the divine will?
options: They are invalid because evil happens in more ways than good does.
They are wrongly assigned because God's actions and commands are fundamentally different.
They are rightly assigned because they mirror how humans show their will to others.
They are only valid for rational creatures and do not apply to the divine will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as humans express their will through actions, permissions, and commands, the same five categories can be used to describe how God's will is made known.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for accepting these five expressions?
options: Augustine stated that God only acts through permission and direct operation.
Humans show their will through direct action, indirect permission, or ordering others.
Scripture explicitly lists these five terms in the Gospel of Matthew.
Rational creatures are the only ones who can understand divine commands.
questions.explanation: Aquinas bases his argument on the analogy of human behavior: we show what we want by doing things ourselves, not stopping others from doing them, or telling others what to do.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the five expressions do not belong to one order?
options: God works in all creatures, so operation and permission apply to everyone equally.
Rational creatures control their own acts, so specific expressions apply to their voluntary actions.
The will of good pleasure is distinct from the will of expression, so they cannot mix.
Evil happens in many ways, so only one expression like prohibition is needed for it.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that because rational beings are masters of their own voluntary acts, God uses specific expressions like precepts and counsel to direct them.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether love exists in God?
options: Love exists in God because He possesses a will.
Love does not exist in God because He has no passions.
Love does not exist in God because He is simple.
Love exists in God only as a metaphor for union.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states we must assert that love is in God because will is in God, and love is the first act of the will.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is love considered the first act of the will?
options: It is the strongest passion that overcomes all others.
It is the only emotion that does not involve bodily change.
It regards good universally, whether possessed or not.
It is the result of knowing universal truth first.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues love is first because it regards good in a universal sense, unlike joy or desire which regard good under specific conditions like possession.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that love implies union, which is impossible in a simple God?
options: Union in God is purely metaphorical and not real.
Love involves willing good for a person, not just physical union.
Love in God is different from love in humans.
God is not actually simple, so union is possible for Him.
questions.explanation: In Reply 3, Aquinas clarifies that love tends toward the good one wills and the person for whom one wills it, defining love as wishing good to someone.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God loves all things equally?
options: God loves some things more than others because He wills a greater good for them.
God does not love created things at all, only His own essence.
God's love is equal in intensity, so He cannot prefer one creature over another.
God loves all things equally because His divine essence is simple and unchanging.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that while the act of God's will is simple, He loves some things more by willing a greater good for them, which explains why some things are better than others.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that God must love some things more than others?
options: Because if God willed equal good for all, no creature would be better than another.
Because the Bible explicitly states that God favors the righteous over the wicked.
Because human beings are inherently superior to animals, demanding more divine affection.
Because God's emotions fluctuate, causing Him to favor certain creatures at different times.
questions.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since God's love causes goodness in things, the existence of varying degrees of goodness implies God wills different amounts of good for different beings.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God has 'equal care' for all things?
options: He claims the scripture is metaphorical and should not be taken literally in theological debates.
He argues that equal care means God gives exactly the same amount of happiness to everyone.
He explains that equal care refers to God's consistent wisdom, not equal distribution of goods.
He states that God's care is equal only for humans, but unequal for animals and plants.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that 'equal care' means God administers all things with the same wisdom and goodness, not that He deals out equal good to all.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God loves better things more?
options: God loves angels more than He loves human beings.
God loves the penitent more than the innocent person.
God always loves the better things more than the lesser ones.
God loves the human race more than He loves Christ.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly answers that it must be so that God loves more the better things, rejecting the objections that suggested otherwise.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God loves better things more?
options: Because better things are physically stronger than lesser things.
Because God is jealous of the higher status of angels.
Because God's will is the cause of goodness in things.
Because the Bible explicitly lists a ranking of all creatures.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God's will causes goodness, and better things have greater good, God necessarily wills (loves) them more.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God loved the human race more than Christ?
options: He claims Christ is actually less good than the whole human race.
He says the Bible verse about Christ is a metaphor, not literal.
He states that God loves the human race and Christ equally.
He argues God loves Christ more than the entire created universe.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas states that God loves Christ more than the whole human race and even more than the entire created universe.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether justice exists in God?
options: Justice does not exist in God because He has no passions or debts.
Justice exists in God in both exchange and distribution, perfectly balanced.
Justice exists in God, but only in the sense of fair distribution, not exchange.
Justice is a human concept that cannot be applied to the divine nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between commutative justice (exchange), which does not apply to God, and distributive justice (giving according to rank), which does apply.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for attributing distributive justice to God?
options: God acts as a ruler who gives each thing what fits its nature and rank.
God owes debts to creation that He pays through natural laws.
God's will is arbitrary, so He defines justice by whatever He chooses.
God engages in mutual trade with humans to establish a moral order.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the order of the universe shows God giving each existing thing what is proper to its condition, similar to a ruler distributing goods.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God is unjust because He does whatever He wills?
options: Justice requires external laws, which God transcends, making the concept irrelevant.
God's will is separate from His wisdom, allowing Him to act outside moral bounds.
God's will is always guided by His wisdom, which serves as His law of justice.
God's will is constrained by human expectations of fairness and reciprocal exchange.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that God cannot will anything His wisdom does not approve, and this wisdom is His law of justice.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the justice of God and truth?
options: God’s justice is a kind of truth, because it follows His wisdom and law.
God’s justice is separate from truth, as justice belongs to the will and truth to the intellect.
God’s justice is a virtue distinct from truth, just like the philosopher says.
God’s justice is only a moral law, not related to truth at all.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says God’s justice, which follows His wisdom, is suitably called truth.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say God’s justice is truth?
options: Because justice is a virtue that is distinct from truth, as the philosopher says.
Because justice is a virtue that aligns actions with the law of God’s wisdom.
Because justice is a virtue that matches the mind’s knowledge of the thing.
Because justice is the rule that makes the mind equal to the thing, just as truth does.
questions.explanation: He compares justice to art: works of justice are true when they follow God’s law, like art follows its rules.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1?
options: He says justice is a virtue distinct from truth, so they are separate.
He says justice resides in the intellect for law, but in the will for commands.
He says justice belongs only to the will, not the intellect.
He says justice is both will and intellect, but they are unrelated.
questions.explanation: His reply: justice is in the intellect for the law, but in the will for the command that governs actions.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether God possesses mercy?
options: God lacks mercy because He is too perfect to experience sadness.
God has mercy only when He breaks His own laws of justice.
God has mercy because He actively removes defects from creatures.
God has mercy because He feels deep sorrow for human suffering.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while God does not feel sorrow (passion), He is merciful because He removes defects and provides goodness to others.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, how does mercy differ from God's justice and liberality?
options: Mercy involves God using good things for His own personal benefit.
Mercy is a relaxation of justice that allows God to deny Himself.
Mercy gives good things in proportion, while justice gives them freely.
Mercy is defined by the removal of defects, not just the giving of good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes mercy specifically by its effect of expelling defects, whereas justice focuses on proportion and liberality on giving without self-interest.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that mercy contradicts God's unchanging justice?
options: He states that God's justice is flexible enough to allow for error.
He claims that justice is secondary and can be overridden by mercy.
He says God ignores His justice when He shows compassion to sinners.
He argues that mercy is doing more than justice requires, not less.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that acting mercifully is doing something extra beyond what justice strictly demands, rather than violating it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main conclusion regarding whether mercy and justice are present in every work of God?
options: Neither is present in the initial act of creation, as these concepts require pre-existing conditions.
Only mercy is present in creation, while justice applies only to the judgment of sins and rewards.
They are mutually exclusive attributes, so God exercises either mercy or justice in any given action.
They are both present in all divine works, though one may appear more prominently than the other in specific cases.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that mercy and justice are necessarily found in all God's works, even if one attribute seems to dominate in certain instances.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, why is mercy considered the foundation for justice in God's actions?
options: Because creation presupposes nothing, making it impossible for justice to exist without mercy first establishing existence.
Because mercy is stronger than justice, allowing God to ignore the debts owed by sinful individuals.
Because any good given to creatures ultimately stems from God's gratuitous goodness, not from what creatures inherently deserve.
Because justice is a human concept that does not apply to God, who acts solely out of compassionate love.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that nothing is due to creatures except by reference to something preceding it, which ultimately traces back to the free gift of divine goodness (mercy).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the affliction of just people in this world proves God lacks justice?
options: He argues that these sufferings cleanse minor faults and help the just detach from earthly things to focus on God.
He states that God's justice is suspended in this life, and true justice will only be applied in the afterlife.
He suggests that the just people are mistaken about their righteousness and are actually being corrected by God.
He claims that the afflictions are actually punishments for hidden sins that the just people have not yet confessed.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states that afflictions purify lesser faults and raise the just from earthly affections toward God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's question?
options: Providence must be attributed to God as the cause of order in created things.
Providence is rejected because it implies a composite nature in God.
Providence is a human concept that cannot apply to an eternal divine being.
Providence is not suitable for God because He never needs to seek advice.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that it is necessary to attribute providence to God because He creates the order found in things.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for attributing providence to God?
options: God must plan for the future because He lacks knowledge of present events.
God acts as a servant who must manage a family or a city effectively.
God uses prudence to resolve doubts about how to guide created beings.
God creates the good order in things, so the plan for that order exists in Him.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God creates the order in things, the 'type' or plan of that order must pre-exist in His mind, which is what providence is.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that providence is not eternal because it deals with temporary things?
options: He denies that providence deals with existing things that are not eternal.
He says the plan of order is eternal, even if its execution happens in time.
He argues that all things God cares for are actually eternal in nature.
He claims that the execution of order is eternal, while the plan is temporary.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas distinguishes between the 'reason of order' (the plan), which is eternal, and the 'execution of order' (government), which is temporal.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether everything is subject to God's providence?
options: Only incorruptible things and human beings are subject to divine providence.
God provides for species generally, but not for individual creatures.
Everything, including individual corruptible things, is subject to divine providence.
Only rational creatures are subject to providence; irrational ones are not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'all things are subject to divine providence, not only in general, but even in their own individual selves,' rejecting the views that limit providence to species or incorruptible things.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming that all things are subject to divine providence?
options: Humans have free will, which requires God's constant oversight to function.
Evil exists only because God allows it, proving He oversees everything.
God knows all things, and knowledge alone implies control over every detail.
God's causality extends to all being, so all things are directed by Him toward an end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God is the first agent whose causality extends to all being, all things are necessarily directed by Him toward an end, which is the definition of providence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God does not care for oxen (Objection 5)?
options: He says that irrational creatures are exempt from divine providence entirely.
He states that God cares for oxen only in their species, not individually.
He argues that rational creatures are specially subject to providence regarding merit and fault.
He claims that oxen are actually rational creatures with free will.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 5, Aquinas explains that rational creatures are subject to providence in an 'especial manner' because they have free will and are accountable for merit or fault, distinguishing their mode of subjection from irrational creatures.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding God's oversight of all things?
options: God delegates all specific governance to angels and celestial bodies.
God only oversees general categories and leaves specific details to other beings.
God has immediate oversight of everything, including the smallest details.
God avoids overseeing vile things to preserve His own dignity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God has immediate providence over everything because He holds the types of all things, even the smallest, in His intellect.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say God uses intermediate causes to govern the world?
options: Because humans need to be ignorant of low things to understand higher ones.
Because God's goodness is so abundant that He shares causal power with creatures.
Because God lacks the power to manage every single detail directly.
Because it is more dignified for a king to have ministers.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God uses intermediaries not due to any defect in His power, but because of the abundance of His goodness, allowing creatures to share in causality.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that a king's dignity requires having ministers?
options: He argues that having ministers proves God is deficient in knowledge.
He says kings lack the plan for their ministers' actions due to their own limits.
He claims that ministers act independently of the king's original plan.
He agrees that God must have ministers to maintain royal dignity.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas notes that while kings have ministers, the fact that they do not know the specific details of those actions stems from a deficiency in the king, not God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God predestines men?
options: Predestination applies only to angels, not to human beings.
God predestines men because He directs rational creatures toward eternal life.
God does not predestine men because human merit depends on our own free choices.
God foreknows human actions but does not predetermine their ultimate end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since eternal life exceeds human nature, God must direct rational creatures toward it, which is the definition of predestination.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why predestination is necessary for humans?
options: God needs to show pity to humans because they are inherently miserable.
Eternal life is beyond human nature, so God must direct us to it.
Predestination ensures that all humans, regardless of merit, reach heaven.
Humans are irrational and need God to force them toward any good end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that because the end of eternal life exceeds the power of created nature, a rational creature must be directed there by another, namely God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that predestination should not be revealed to everyone?
options: Predestination is a secret that even the Holy Ghost cannot reveal to humans.
Only the Pope is allowed to know who is predestined to maintain order.
Revealing it would cause despair in the non-predestined and laziness in the predestined.
It is revealed to everyone through the Holy Spirit to ensure universal salvation.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 4, Aquinas states that revealing predestination to all would lead those not chosen to despair and those chosen to become negligent.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, where does predestination actually exist?
options: In the future glory that the chosen will eventually receive
In the mind of God as a plan for ordering souls
In the physical world as a change happening to the chosen
In the minds of the people who are chosen for salvation
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that predestination is not in the predestined but only in the person who predestines, specifically as a type or plan existing in the divine mind.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying predestination is not in the predestined?
options: Because God’s actions never cause any change in the things they act upon
Because the people predestined do not exist yet when God makes the decision
Because grace is a temporal thing and cannot be part of an eternal definition
Because predestination is a part of providence, which is a mental plan, not a physical effect
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that predestination is part of providence, which is a 'type in the mind of the provider,' distinct from the execution of that plan which happens in the things governed.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that predestination is a 'preparation' found in the thing prepared?
options: He claims that the objection confuses predestination with the actual act of calling
He argues that preparation is only a temporary state that disappears after grace
He agrees that preparation is always found in the object being prepared
He says preparation can mean the agent’s mental planning, which stays in the agent
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that preparation can refer to the agent preparing itself to act by conceiving the idea, which remains in the agent rather than the object.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God reprobates any person?
options: God reprobates no one because He loves all things He has created.
God does not reprobate anyone, but merely foresees who will sin.
God does reprobate some people, allowing them to fall into sin and face damnation.
God reprobates everyone who fails to achieve eternal life through their own efforts.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'God does reprobate some' as part of His providence, permitting them to fall away from the end of eternal life.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God reprobates some individuals?
options: It is part of divine providence to permit certain defects and allow some to turn aside from salvation.
Reprobation is necessary to balance the number of people who are predestined for heaven.
God hates those who reject Him, which forces them into a state of reprobation.
God actively causes people to sin so that He can demonstrate His power over them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as providence ordains some to salvation, it also permits some to fall away; reprobation is this permission within God's overall plan.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 1, how does Aquinas explain that God can love all men yet still reprobate some?
options: God loves all men equally, but reprobation is a mistake in His divine plan that He corrects later.
God's love is directed only at the soul, while reprobation affects only the physical body.
God's love is conditional, meaning He stops loving those who commit serious sins against Him.
God loves all by wishing them some good, but He does not wish the specific good of eternal life for all.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that God wishes some good for everyone (love), but He does not wish the particular good of eternal life for everyone (reprobation).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the predestined are chosen by God?
options: No, God's goodness is shared equally with all, so no specific choice is made.
Yes, everyone who is predestined is also an object of God's election and love.
Yes, but only for those who already exist at the moment of predestination.
No, predestination happens before any act of choosing or loving by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly concludes that 'all the predestinate are objects of election and love,' rejecting the idea that predestination occurs without these prior acts.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why predestination must involve election and love?
options: Because directing things toward a goal requires a prior will to achieve that goal.
Because election is necessary to ensure that God's justice is visibly demonstrated to all.
Because God must choose specific individuals to distinguish them from the rest of humanity.
Because love must precede election in God, just as it does in human decision-making.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that predestination is part of providence (directing things to an end), and nothing is directed to an end unless the will for that end already exists, which entails love and election.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God wills all men to be saved, implying no specific choice?
options: He claims that God's will is too complex to be understood by human logic.
He states that predestination overrides the general will to save every single person.
He argues that the biblical quote is metaphorical and does not apply to divine action.
He says God's will to save all is a relative desire, not a simple, effective will.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas distinguishes between God's 'antecedent will' (willing relatively that all be saved) and his 'consequent will' (willing simply/effectively), explaining how both can be true.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God's foreknowledge of human merits causes predestination?
options: Foreknowledge of merits is the primary cause, but God's will is the secondary cause.
No merit, whether past, present, or future, is the cause of God's decision to predestine anyone.
God predestines people because he foresees they will earn salvation through their own good works.
Only merits from a previous life cause predestination, while current merits do not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the idea that any merit (past, present, or future) causes predestination, stating that the cause must be sought in God's will and goodness, not human action.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the ultimate reason or foundation for God's act of predestination?
options: The desire to reward those who show initial willingness to accept grace.
The need to maintain justice by giving unequal rewards to unequal people.
The inherent equality of all human beings in nature and original sin.
The goodness of God, which seeks to represent itself in created things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that predestination is founded on the goodness of God, who creates and predestines to manifest his goodness, rather than responding to human merit.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 1 (which cites Romans 8:29), how does Aquinas explain the relationship between foreknown grace and predestination?
options: Foreknowledge of using grace well is the efficient cause that forces God to give grace.
Foreknowledge of using grace well is a final cause, not the efficient cause of giving grace.
The verse means God predestines only those who have already proven their worthiness.
Aquinas agrees with the objection that foreknowledge is the direct cause of predestination.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that while God foresees how grace will be used, this foresight acts as a final cause (purpose), not the efficient cause that brings about the gift of grace itself.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the certainty of predestination?
options: It is certain and infallible, but it does not force people to act against their free will.
It is necessary in the strict sense, meaning the outcome happens out of absolute compulsion.
It is only probable, as human free will can easily override divine planning.
It is uncertain because God could have chosen different people to save in the past.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that predestination takes effect most certainly and infallibly, yet it does not impose necessity, meaning it does not destroy human free will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why predestination is certain without being coercive?
options: God's will is immutable, so He cannot change His mind once He has predestined someone.
Human merit ensures the outcome, making the result dependent on the individual's actions.
The effects of predestination are necessary because they are part of the divine nature.
Divine providence is infallible, but it allows events to happen through contingent causes like free will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that while the order of providence is infallible, it permits contingency through proximate causes, such as free will, so the effect is certain but not necessary.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a predestined person might lose their 'crown' by sinning?
options: The crown is lost only if earned by merit, which can be forfeited, but not if held by predestination.
The crown is always lost if a person commits a mortal sin, regardless of predestination.
The objection is invalid because no one can actually lose their crown once it is given.
Predestination is conditional, so the crown is only secure if the person never sins.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas distinguishes between holding the crown by predestination (which is secure) and holding it by merit (which can be lost through sin).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of people predestined for salvation?
options: The number is fixed, but it is smaller than the number of people who are lost.
The number is certain in general size, but God does not know which specific individuals are saved.
The number is certain both in its total amount and in the specific individuals included.
The number is uncertain because God can always add more people to it.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly rejects the idea that the number is only formally certain (general size) but not materially certain (specific individuals). He argues that for God, the number is certain in both aspects.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that God has a definite number of predestined people?
options: Because the Bible explicitly states a specific number of people who will be saved.
Because every agent, including God, intends a specific finite result for the essential parts of their work.
Because God’s knowledge is limited, so He must set a fixed quota for salvation.
Because nature shows that good things are always the majority, so God must save most people.
questions.explanation: Aquinas uses the analogy of a builder who plans specific measurements for a house. He argues that God, as an agent, intends a definite measure for the essential parts of the universe, which includes the number of rational creatures attaining eternal happiness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God might add more people to the number of the saved?
options: He states that the objection is valid and that the number of the predestined is indeed uncertain.
He claims that the number of the saved is actually infinite, so adding more makes no difference.
He argues that God changes His mind occasionally, so the number fluctuates based on human actions.
He says the biblical reference applies to those currently righteous, whose numbers change, not the final predestined.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the scripture about adding to the number refers to people marked out for present righteousness, which can increase or decrease, rather than the fixed number of the predestined.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the role of saints' prayers in predestination?
options: Prayers are useless because God's decision is fixed and unchangeable.
Prayers can stop God from predestining someone to eternal salvation.
Prayers do not cause the decree but help fulfill its intended effect.
Prayers change God's eternal decree to save specific individuals.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between the divine decree itself, which is eternal and unchangeable, and its effect, which is brought about through secondary causes like prayer.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why prayers can help with predestination?
options: Prayers provide God with new information that He did not previously know.
God uses secondary causes, like prayers, to bring about the effects He predestined.
God lacks the power to save people without the assistance of human prayers.
The saints have more authority than God, so their prayers override His will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God's providence works through secondary causes, meaning He predestines salvation in a way that includes human actions like prayer as necessary means.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that if predestination can be helped, it can also be hindered?
options: He claims that predestination is too weak to be affected by any human action.
He argues that hindrance is possible only for people who are not predestined.
He states that secondary causes execute God's order and cannot oppose it.
He agrees that human actions can sometimes block God's eternal plan.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that secondary causes operate within God's universal order, so they can further predestination but cannot impede it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between the 'book of life' and predestination?
options: They are the same thing, viewed from different angles: one is the choice itself, the other is God's knowledge of that choice.
They are distinct concepts, with the book of life referring to scripture and predestination to God's power.
The book of life is a physical record kept by angels, while predestination is an abstract divine idea.
They are unrelated; the book of life lists all humans, whereas predestination applies only to the saints.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the book of life is metaphorical for God's knowledge of those He has predestined, meaning they are the same reality considered from the perspective of the choice versus the knowledge of that choice.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for calling God's knowledge of the predestined the 'book of life'?
options: It reflects the idea that divine energy actively recalls good works, similar to how books store information.
It mirrors human custom where chosen individuals are recorded in lists, symbolizing firm memory and selection.
God literally writes names in a physical book to ensure no one is forgotten in the afterlife.
The term comes from ancient laws requiring soldiers to sign a contract before entering eternal service.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as humans record chosen individuals in books to signify selection and aid memory, God's firm knowledge of those chosen for eternal life is metaphorically called the 'book of life'.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that there should be a 'book of death' corresponding to reprobation?
options: He argues that reprobation is not a choice but a failure, so it does not require any form of record.
He states that custom dictates recording those who are chosen, not those who are rejected, so no book of death exists.
He claims the book of death exists but is destroyed immediately after judgment, leaving no permanent record.
He admits there is a book of death, but it is hidden from human view to prevent despair.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that the practice of inscription applies to those who are chosen, not those who are rejected; therefore, there is no corresponding 'book of death' for the reprobate.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding what the 'book of life' refers to?
options: It refers to both natural life and the life of grace.
It refers to God's own natural life and knowledge.
It refers to the initial choice of the twelve apostles.
It refers strictly to the life of glory for the chosen.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that strictly speaking, the book of life regards the life of glory, as this is the ultimate end for which humans are chosen.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for limiting the 'book of life' to the life of glory?
options: Grace is a natural gift that everyone receives by birth.
Glory is the final end that exceeds human nature.
God's own life is the only true source of all existence.
Natural life is not considered a form of divine election.
questions.explanation: He argues that election implies choosing for an end that is not natural, and the life of glory is the specific end that exceeds human nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that some are chosen for grace but not for glory?
options: Grace is the primary end to which glory is merely directed.
Grace is a natural attribute that requires no divine choice.
The objection is false because all chosen receive glory immediately.
Grace is a means to an end, not the end itself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that the life of grace is directed toward glory, so one is only chosen for grace insofar as it leads to the final end of glory.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, can a person be removed from the book of life?
options: No, because once written, a name is indelibly fixed forever.
No, because God's foreknowledge is perfect and never changes.
Yes, but only because human opinion about them changes.
Yes, if a person falls from a state of grace through mortal sin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the predestined cannot be removed, those written in the book due to current grace can be 'blotted out' if they lose that grace through sin.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying someone can be blotted out?
options: Predestination is temporary and can be revoked by God.
The book of life is merely a human record of reputation.
The person's relationship to eternal life changes by losing grace.
God changes His mind about who deserves eternal life.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states the blotting out refers to the thing known (the person) changing by falling from grace, not to any change in God's eternal knowledge.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God's foreknowledge cannot be changed?
options: He admits that God's foreknowledge can be deceived by human action.
He argues that foreknowledge is not the same as the book of life.
He claims God's foreknowledge is actually mutable in some cases.
He says the change is in the person, not in God's knowledge.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that blotting out refers to the foreknown things changing, not to any change occurring within God's immutable foreknowledge.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether God has power?
options: God has neither active nor passive power
God has both active and passive power equally
God has active power but no passive power
God has passive power but no active power
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that passive power is absent in God, while active power belongs to Him in the highest degree.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God having active power?
options: God is like primary matter, which is the basis of power
God is deficient in some ways, requiring potentiality to act
God's will is distinct from His essence, creating a gap
God is pure act and perfect, making Him an active principle
questions.explanation: Because God is pure act and perfectly complete, He functions as an active principle, which corresponds to active power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God's action is better than His power?
options: He claims that passive power is actually better than active power
He says that God's power is accidental, so it is not His essence
He argues that in God, action and power are the same essence
He agrees that action is nobler, so power cannot exist in God
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that the objection assumes action and power are distinct; in God, they are identical, so one is not 'better' than the other.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God's power is infinite?
options: God's power is finite because infinite things are imperfect.
God's power is unknown because it produces no infinite effects.
God's power is limited to ensure the universe has a beginning.
God's power is infinite because His very being is infinite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God's essence (His existence) is infinite, His active power must also be infinite.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for God having infinite power?
options: The sun's power is infinite, so God's power must be greater.
Infinite power is required to move spiritual creatures through time.
An infinite effect proves that the cause must have infinite power.
Power depends on the perfection of the agent's essence, which is infinite.
questions.explanation: He reasons that an agent's power corresponds to how perfectly it possesses the form by which it acts; since God's essence is infinite, His power is too.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that infinite power would cause instantaneous movement?
options: The objection applies to physical bodies, not to God's spiritual nature.
The objection is wrong because God moves things in space and time.
God does cause instantaneous movement, but we cannot perceive it.
Infinite power only causes instantaneous movement in spiritual creatures.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that the philosopher's proof about instantaneous movement applies specifically to corporeal (physical) things, whereas God is not a body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is omnipotent?
options: God is omnipotent because He can perform any action, even those that are logically contradictory.
God is omnipotent because He can do everything that is logically possible for a being to do.
God is omnipotent only in the sense that He can do what human beings are capable of doing.
God is not omnipotent because He is unable to move or be affected by external forces.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that God is omnipotent because He can do all things that are 'absolutely possible,' meaning actions that do not involve a logical contradiction or impossibility.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot do certain things?
options: Such actions are logically impossible because they involve a contradiction in terms.
God lacks the physical strength to perform actions that require movement or change.
God chooses not to do them because they would interfere with human free will.
These actions are impossible because they are beyond the scope of created nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God cannot do things that are 'absolutely impossible,' which are actions where the description is self-contradictory, such as making a square circle.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God cannot sin, and therefore is not omnipotent?
options: He claims that sin is not an action at all, so it does not count as a limit on power.
He states that God can sin, but chooses not to in order to maintain moral order in the world.
He says that God's power is limited by divine law, which forbids Him from committing evil.
He argues that sin is a lack of perfection, so the inability to sin proves God's perfect power.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that sin is a falling short of perfect action; thus, being unable to sin is a sign of omnipotence, not a lack of it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can make the past not to have been?
options: God can do this, but only for minor historical events.
God cannot do this because it involves a logical contradiction.
God can do this if He chooses to change His own mind.
God can do this because His power is unlimited and absolute.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that making the past not to have been implies a contradiction (something both happened and did not happen), which falls outside the scope of divine power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot undo the past?
options: God's power is limited by the natural laws of time and space.
It is logically impossible for something to have happened and not happened at the same time.
Changing the past would make God's knowledge of the future incorrect.
It would violate the free will of the people who performed the past actions.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that saying an event both happened and did not happen is a contradiction, similar to saying someone is sitting and not sitting simultaneously.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God can restore lost virtues like charity, so He should be able to undo past corruption?
options: God can remove the current effects of sin, but cannot erase the fact that it occurred.
God can remove the guilt of sin, but not the physical consequences.
The objection is wrong because charity cannot be lost in the first place.
Charity is different from virginity, so the comparison is invalid.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states that while God can remove the corruption itself, He cannot remove the fact that the corruption once existed.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can do things other than what He actually does?
options: God can do other things than those He has actually done.
God only acts out of natural necessity, like a seed growing into a plant.
God cannot do what He has not already foreknown and pre-ordained.
God is limited to the current order of events and cannot create anything else.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states at the end of his answer that 'God can do other things than those He has done,' rejecting the idea that He is bound to the current course of events.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God is not restricted to the present order of things?
options: Divine goodness is so vast that it exceeds any specific order of created things.
God's will is naturally determined to produce only what currently exists.
The current order of things is the only one that is just and good.
God's power is separate from His wisdom, allowing Him to act freely.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because divine goodness is an end that exceeds all proportion to created things, divine wisdom is not restricted to any particular order of events.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God cannot do what is not good for creatures?
options: He claims that creatures are not bound by the laws of divine justice.
He agrees that no other order would be suitable for the things that now exist.
He argues that God's power and wisdom are not restricted to the current order.
He states that the current order is the only one that fits divine wisdom.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that while the current order is restricted to what exists, God's power and wisdom are not, so He can impose another order.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can do better than what He currently does?
options: God cannot do better because doing so would imply that His original wisdom was flawed or envious.
God can make the exact same individual thing better in every single aspect of its existence.
God can create different things that are better than any specific created thing, but cannot change a thing's core nature.
God is unable to create anything superior to the existing universe because it is already perfect.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that while God cannot make a specific thing 'better' in a way that changes its essential definition (like making the number four into five), He can always create a different thing that is better than any given created thing.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God cannot make a specific thing better in its core nature?
options: Because God’s power is limited by the laws of nature that He established at creation.
Because created things are already at the highest possible level of goodness allowed for creation.
Because changing the core nature of a thing would destroy the beautiful order of the universe.
Because a thing’s essential goodness is defined by what it is, so changing that makes it a different thing.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that essential goodness is tied to a thing's definition. If you add a substantial difference to make it 'better,' it ceases to be that specific thing and becomes something else, similar to how adding one to the number four makes it five.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the universe cannot be better because it already has the most beautiful order?
options: He claims that God can improve the order by making all things equally good, removing any hierarchy.
He agrees that the universe is perfect and therefore no single part can be improved without breaking the harmony.
He argues that the beauty of the universe depends on the specific proportions between things, so improving one would ruin the balance.
He states that the universe is not actually beautiful, but only appears so to human observers.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the universe's goodness lies in its ordered proportions. If one part were made better, it would disrupt the relative balance, like stretching one string of a harp too much, which would ruin the music.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether beatitude belongs to God?
options: Beatitude belongs to God only as a reward for His virtues.
Beatitude belongs to God in the highest and most excellent degree.
Beatitude is a concept that applies to creatures but not to God.
Beatitude does not belong to God because He lacks composition of goods.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that beatitude belongs to God in a very special and highest manner because God possesses perfect goodness and intelligence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying beatitude belongs to God?
options: God is a perfect intellectual nature that fully possesses the good.
God aggregates all good things together in a complex way.
God is the only being capable of experiencing good or ill.
God earns beatitude by performing virtuous actions over time.
questions.explanation: Aquinas defines beatitude as the perfect good of an intellectual nature, and since God is perfectly good and intelligent, beatitude belongs to Him.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God cannot have beatitude because He lacks the 'aggregation' of goods?
options: God does not need aggregation because He is not an intellectual nature.
God possesses all goods in a simple, unified way rather than as parts.
Aggregation only applies to physical objects, not to spiritual beings like God.
God aggregates goods through His actions in the world, not within Himself.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas argues that what is manifold in creatures pre-exists in God in simplicity and unity, not as a composition.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is called blessed in respect of His intellect?
options: No, because goodness refers to God's essence rather than His thinking.
Yes, because understanding is the highest activity of an intellectual nature.
Yes, but only because God's will rests in His intellectual perfection.
No, because happiness is an end that belongs to the will, not the mind.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that beatitude must be assigned to God in respect of His intellect because intellectual operation (understanding) is the most perfect activity of an intellectual nature.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for linking God's blessedness to His intellect?
options: Intellectual creatures naturally desire to grasp everything, which God does perfectly.
The will desires happiness, so the intellect must precede the will in God's nature.
Goodness is defined by being, which is found primarily in God's essence, not mind.
In God, existence and understanding are identical, making understanding the core of His being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since beatitude is the perfect good of an intellectual nature, and the most perfect act of such a nature is understanding, God's beatitude lies in His intellect, where being and understanding are one.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that beatitude belongs to the will because it is an end?
options: He claims that the intellect is the end, not the will, in God.
He agrees that the will is primary, but says the intellect supports it.
He says the object of the will is understood before the will's act.
He argues that the will is not an end, but a means to happiness.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that since beatitude is the object of the will, and objects are understood as prior to the act of the power, divine beatitude (intellect) precedes the act of the will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is the beatitude of the blessed?
options: God is the beatitude only as the object known, while the act of knowing is created.
Beatitude is entirely a created thing, and God is merely the cause of it.
The beatitude of the blessed is identical to God's own uncreated happiness.
God is the sole and complete beatitude in every possible sense for every blessed person.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between the object (God) and the act (understanding). He concludes God is the beatitude as the object, but the act of understanding is a created perfection in the blessed.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas distinguish between the object of understanding and the act of understanding?
options: To show that while God is the thing known, the human act of knowing is created.
To prove that the act of knowing is more important than the object known.
To demonstrate that created beings can achieve an uncreated state of happiness.
To argue that God cannot be the object of human understanding in this life.
questions.explanation: Aquinas uses this distinction to resolve the tension: God is the supreme good as the object, but the act of enjoying Him is a created good within the creature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that there cannot be many supreme goods?
options: The objection is wrong because God is not actually the supreme good.
There is only one supreme good, which is the act of understanding, not God.
Multiple supreme goods can exist if they are shared by different people.
God is the supreme good absolutely, but the act of beatitude is supreme only for creatures.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas clarifies that beatitude is the supreme good absolutely regarding its object (God), but only relatively supreme regarding the act, which is a created participation.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God's happiness includes all other forms of happiness?
options: God's happiness contains the perfect essence of every desirable thing found in other forms of happiness.
Only true happiness is found in God, while false happiness exists entirely outside of Him.
God's happiness is distinct and separate from all human or earthly forms of happiness.
God's happiness is limited to spiritual matters and excludes physical pleasures or riches.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that whatever is desirable in any beatitude, true or false, pre-exists wholly and in a higher degree in the divine beatitude.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying God's beatitude includes earthly goods like riches or power?
options: God allows humans to have these goods so they can eventually understand His nature.
God possesses the perfect spiritual equivalents of these goods, such as self-sufficiency and omnipotence.
Earthly goods are illusions, and God's happiness is the only reality that truly matters.
God created these earthly goods, so He must possess them in their physical form as well.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that God has complete self-sufficiency instead of riches, omnipotence instead of power, and so on, possessing the perfect form of what these goods promise.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God cannot contain 'false' happiness because nothing false is in God?
options: False happiness is completely absent from God, but its small resemblance to true happiness exists in Him.
False happiness is a human invention that has no connection to God's nature at all.
There is no such thing as false happiness; all happiness is ultimately true and divine.
God contains false happiness to show His power over evil and deception.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that while the specific false beatitude is not in God, whatever slight semblance it has of true beatitude pre-exists in Him.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the possibility of procession in God?
options: Procession exists in God, but only as an inward, intellectual act.
There is no procession in God.
Procession is a human concept that cannot apply to God.
Procession exists only outwardly, not inwardly.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says that while outward procession is absent, an inward, intelligible procession exists within God.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say that outward procession is impossible in God?
options: Because God is immobile and has no external effects.
Because God’s nature forbids any action toward external matter.
Because God is too simple to have any movement at all.
Because God is not a body and therefore cannot move.
questions.explanation: He explains that procession implies outward movement, which God lacks because He is immobile and has no external effects.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 2 (about distinctness of what proceeds)?
options: He agrees that anything that proceeds must be distinct from its source.
He says that inward procession can be closely united with its source.
He claims that outward procession is the only true procession.
He argues that procession always creates a new, separate entity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that inward procession need not be distinct; the more perfect the procession, the closer it is to its source.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the article's question?
options: Only the creation of the world can be called generation in God.
No internal process in God can be called generation because God does not change.
The process of the Word in God is properly called generation.
Generation in God is only a metaphor and not a real event.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that the procession of the Word in God is called generation.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for calling this process generation?
options: It involves a change from non-existence to existence within the divine nature.
It is the only process in God that involves physical matter and change.
It creates a new, separate substance that is distinct from the Father.
It proceeds from a living principle by way of likeness in the same nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that generation in living things involves origin from a conjoined principle by way of similitude in the same nature, which applies to the Word.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that generated existence cannot be self-subsisting?
options: He agrees that the Son is not self-subsisting but depends on the Father.
He denies that the Son's existence is derived from the Father at all.
He argues that derived existence does not always mean existing in another subject.
He claims that divine existence is actually derived from a prior non-existent state.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that not everything derived from another has existence in another subject, refuting the claim that derived existence precludes self-subsistence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of processions in God?
options: Processions in God are infinite because God's nature is infinite.
There are three processions corresponding to the three Persons of the Trinity.
There is only one procession, which is the generation of the Word.
There are two processions: the Word and the procession of Love.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that there are two processions in God: the procession of the Word and the procession of Love.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for a second procession existing in God?
options: The operation of the will involves a procession of love, distinct from the intellect.
The first procession must be followed by another to avoid logical contradiction.
God has two distinct natures that require separate modes of communication.
Love is a stronger force than understanding, requiring its own origin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that just as the intellect produces the Word, the will produces Love, and since both operations remain within the agent, both constitute processions.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that admitting a second procession leads to an infinite chain?
options: He claims that infinity is possible in God because God is not limited by time.
He states that the first procession is so complete it excludes any further movement.
He argues that the chain stops because the will's procession is the final internal act.
He suggests that the second procession is actually the same as the first.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that the procession within an intellectual nature terminates in the procession of the will, so there is no need to go on to infinity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the question of whether the procession of love in God is generation?
options: The procession of love in God is identical to the production of the Word.
The procession of love in God is not generation, but rather a movement.
The procession of love in God is indeed a form of generation.
The procession of love in God is a type of birth similar to human reproduction.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that the procession of love in God ought not to be called generation, but rather proceeds as spirit, expressing a vital movement.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why love does not proceed by way of generation?
options: Because the will moves toward an object by inclination, not by creating a likeness.
Because love is an external force that separates the divine nature from itself.
Because the intellect is the only faculty that can produce a new being in God.
Because generation requires a physical body, which God does not possess.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the will is activated by an inclination toward the object, not by a similitude (likeness) residing within it, whereas generation requires the production of a likeness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that 'every beast loves its like,' suggesting love proceeds by likeness?
options: Likeness is the principle that causes love, but love itself is not a likeness.
Love is a likeness of the object, just as the Word is a likeness of the Father.
The objection is valid, but the term 'generation' is simply the wrong word to use.
Beasts do not actually love their like, so the biblical quote is misleading.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that while likeness is the principle of loving, love itself is not a likeness in the same way the Word is.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of processions in God?
options: There are three processions, adding power to intellect and will.
There are many processions, as God's power exceeds human capacity.
There is only one procession, since God is perfectly simple.
There are exactly two processions: one from intellect and one from will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that only the acts of intelligence and will remain within the agent, resulting in exactly two processions: the Word and Love.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that only two processions exist in God?
options: Because only intellect and will are actions that remain entirely within the agent.
Because sensation is an intellectual act that produces a third internal movement.
Because God's simplicity prevents any action from remaining within Himself.
Because power and goodness are external attributes that do not originate inside God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that divine processions come from actions remaining within the agent, and in an intellectual nature, only intelligence and will fit this description.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God's power should imply a third procession?
options: Power relates to external action on others, not to an internal divine person.
God's power is too great to be limited to just two internal movements.
Power is actually a form of will, so it is already included in Love.
Power proceeds from goodness, which is the true source of all procession.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that power is the principle for acting on another, so it points to external creation, not to an internal procession of a divine person.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the existence of real relations within God?
options: Relations in God are real only when they involve different natures, such as creator and creature.
No real relations exist in God because everything in Him refers to His substance.
Real relations do exist in God because divine processions share the same nature.
Relations in God are only logical constructs found in the mind, not in reality.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that relations exist in God really because the divine processions occur within the identity of the same nature, creating a mutual order.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why these relations are real rather than just logical?
