questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding the use of general divine attributes for specific persons?
options: It should be avoided because it risks creating errors in the faith.
It is wrong because one person cannot act as a form for another person.
It is fitting to assign general attributes to specific persons to help reveal the Trinity.
It is impossible because general attributes exist before specific persons in our understanding.
questions.explanation: Aquinas answers the article's question by stating that it is fitting for essential attributes to be appropriated to persons for the manifestation of faith.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for appropriating these attributes to the persons?
options: General attributes are easier for us to understand than the specific properties of the persons.
The attributes belong exclusively to the persons to whom they are assigned.
The Trinity can be proven by logical demonstration using these attributes.
The personal properties are more clearly known to us through created things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that essential attributes are clearer to human reason than personal properties, so they are used to make the persons manifest.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that assigning attributes to persons might cause heresy?
options: By arguing that the Trinity can be proven by demonstration, removing doubt.
By rejecting the idea that attributes signify by mode of form.
By stating that the attributes are actually prior to the persons in reality.
By clarifying that the attributes are not exclusive to the persons but used for likeness.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that attributes are not assigned as exclusive possessions but to manifest the persons, preventing error.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the way holy doctors assign divine attributes to the Persons of the Trinity?
options: They assign them unfittingly because the attributes belong to the divine essence, not the Persons.
They assign them fittingly because the attributes resemble the specific properties of each Person.
They assign them arbitrarily because human language cannot accurately describe God's nature.
They assign them inconsistently because different doctors like Hilary and Augustine disagree.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the appropriations are fitting because the attributes (like eternity or beauty) have a natural likeness to the properties of the Father, Son, or Holy Spirit.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas believe our minds can appropriately link certain attributes to specific Persons of the Trinity?
options: Because the attributes are actually distinct parts of God that correspond to the three Persons.
Because the Bible explicitly commands us to associate specific words with each Person of the Trinity.
Because each Person possesses a different part of the divine essence, requiring different descriptive terms.
Because we understand God through creatures, and the attributes mirror how we perceive being, unity, and relation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that our intellect moves from creatures to God, considering being, unity, power, and relation; the appropriated attributes mirror this fourfold order of understanding.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain why 'beauty' (species) is fittingly appropriated to the Son?
options: Beauty implies eternal duration, which matches the Son as the uncreated source of all things.
Beauty implies strength and power, which matches the Son as the active force of creation.
Beauty implies joyful enjoyment, which matches the Son as the love shared between Father and Spirit.
Beauty implies perfection and harmony, which matches the Son as the perfect Image and Word of the Father.
questions.explanation: Aquinas links beauty to integrity (perfection), proportion (harmony/image), and clarity (light/word), all of which correspond to the Son's property as the perfect Image and Word.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between divine relations and persons?
options: Relations are not the same as persons because they point outward.
Relations are the same as persons but do not exist in them.
Relations are distinct entities that exist alongside the persons.
Relations are identical to persons and exist within them.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the divine essence is the same as the person, and relation is the divine essence, relation must be the same as the person. He further states that properties are 'in' the persons, just as a form is in its subject.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why relation is the same as person?
options: Persons are multiplied by relations, proving their fundamental unity.
Relations signify existence toward something, which defines the person.
Nothing can be contained by itself, so relation must be the person.
The divine essence is identical to the person, and relation is that essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas bases his conclusion on the premise that in God, the relation is really the divine essence itself. Since he has already established that the essence is the same as the person, the relation must also be the same as the person.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that if relation and person were identical, relation would be in the essence?
options: He claims that relation is not in the essence because it points toward others.
He says relation is in the essence only by identity, but in persons by identity and mode.
He argues that the essence is not a person, so relation cannot be in it.
He states that the objection is invalid because persons are not contained by themselves.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas distinguishes between how properties relate to the essence (by mode of identity only) and how they relate to persons (by mode of identity and signification, like a form in a subject).

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude is the principle that distinguishes the divine persons from one another?
options: The origin or act of generation, which shows how one person comes from another.
The relations, such as paternity and filiation, which constitute the persons themselves.
The divine essence, which is shared by all three persons in common.
The absolute nature of God, which exists prior to any relative distinctions.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the persons share the same essence, they must be distinguished by relations, which are intrinsic and constitutive of the persons.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas reject 'origin' (like generation) as the primary principle of distinction?
options: Origin is a relative term that presupposes a distinction that already exists.
Origin implies that the divine persons are not simple but are composed of parts.
Origin describes a movement or path between persons, not an intrinsic quality within them.
Origin is too vague to account for the specific differences between Father and Son.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that origin signifies a 'way from' or 'to' something, rather than an intrinsic property that makes the persons distinct in themselves.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that relations presuppose distinction and thus cannot be its source?
options: In God, relations are not accidental but subsistent, so they create the distinction rather than relying on it.
Distinction comes from matter in creatures, but in God it comes from the divine will.
Relations in God are absolute, not relative, so they do not refer to another person at all.
The objection is valid for creatures but not for God, because God is beyond logic.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that while accidental relations presuppose distinct subjects, subsistent relations (like in God) actually bring about the distinction.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the distinct persons of God remain if their specific relational properties are removed from our mental concept?
options: The persons remain as long as the non-relational attributes like being unbegotten are kept.
The persons remain because they are defined by their origin rather than their relations.
The persons remain because the divine essence is independent of any relational distinctions.
The persons do not remain because the relations are what make each person distinct.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that if the personal relations are mentally abstracted, the hypostases (persons) no longer remain because the relations constitute their distinctness.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why removing personal relations causes the distinct persons to disappear from our understanding?
options: The persons are universal concepts that can be understood even when specific particular details are taken away.
The relations are merely accidental properties that do not define the core identity of the divine substance.
The relations are like forms added to a pre-existing subject, so removing them leaves the subject intact.
The relations are not added to the persons but are identical to them, so removing them removes the person.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that personal properties are not additions to the persons but are the persons themselves, so abstracting the relation abstracts the person.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the Father could be called 'unbegotten' even if He had not begotten the Son?
options: He claims that 'unbegotten' is a positive property that remains even when paternity is abstracted.
He states that Augustine meant the Father would cease to exist if He did not beget the Son.
He argues that 'unbegotten' is a negation and does not actually constitute or distinguish the Father.
He agrees that 'unbegotten' is a sufficient definition of the Father if paternity is removed.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that 'being unbegotten' is a negation, not a positive property that constitutes the hypostasis.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, when we consider how the Father's personal identity (paternity) is established, what is the logical order between the act of begetting and the property of being the Father?
options: They occur simultaneously, with neither logically preceding the other in our understanding.
The act of begetting comes first, because an action requires a person to perform it.
The property of being the Father comes first, because it defines the nature of God.
The property of being the Father comes first, because the person must exist to act.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that when considering how a person is constituted, the personal property (like paternity) must precede the notional act (like begetting), just as a person must exist before they can perform an action.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying that the personal property precedes the notional act in the order of intelligence?
options: Because the Son's birth is the primary cause of the Father's identity.
Because an action logically presupposes a person who is acting.
Because relations are always founded upon the actions that create them.
Because the Father's existence is independent of any generative process.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the notional act presupposes the relation when the relation constitutes the person, because an action presupposes a person acting.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that claims 'because He begets, He is Father' proves generation precedes paternity?
options: He says the objection is correct only if we ignore the Holy Spirit's procession.
He argues that the objection confuses the Father's role with the Son's role in generation.
He claims that the Master of the Sentences was referring to human fathers, not God.
He explains that the objection treats 'Father' as a mere relation, not as a subsisting person.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that the quote treats 'Father' as a relation only; if it signified the subsisting person, the logic would be reversed.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the notional acts and the divine persons?
options: They should be attributed to the persons to show how they originate.
They belong to God's essence, not to the specific persons.
They are identical to the relations and thus need no separate name.
They are rejected because actions naturally involve suffering.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his 'I answer that' section that we must attribute notional acts to the persons to signify the order of origin.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for attributing these acts to the persons?
options: To indicate the specific order in which the persons originate.
To prove that God has passions similar to human beings.
To distinguish the persons based on their shared divine substance.
To separate the acts from the relations of the persons.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that distinction among divine persons is founded on origin, and origin can only be properly designated by these specific acts.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that actions naturally cause suffering (passion) in God?
options: He states that the type of action causing suffering is not attributed to God.
He claims that divine actions do not involve any kind of movement.
He agrees that God suffers, but only in a grammatical sense.
He argues that suffering is actually a necessary part of divine origin.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas clarifies that the specific sense of action that implies movement and passion is not what is attributed to God.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the Father's begetting of the Son is an act of will?
options: It is both an act of will and nature, since God wills everything He does by nature.
It is not an act of will in the sense that will is the source of the action; it is an act of nature.
It is an act of will, but only in the sense that the Father desires to be the Father.
It is an act of will because the Father freely chose to create the Son as a unique being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between will as a mere accompaniment and will as a principle of action. He concludes that while God wills to beget, the begetting itself proceeds from nature, not will, because nature is determined to one effect.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying the Son is begotten by nature rather than by will?
options: Nature produces only one specific result, whereas will can choose among many different possibilities.
Nature is necessary and unchangeable, while will is free and changeable in its decisions.
Will is a higher faculty than nature, so it cannot be the source of divine generation.
God's nature is simple and unified, while His will is complex and divided.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that nature is determined to one specific outcome (like fire heating), whereas will is not determined to one thing but can choose among many options based on understanding. Since the Son is a unique, necessary result, it comes from nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the Son is the 'Son of His love' (Colossians 1:13)?
options: The phrase is metaphorical and does not apply to the divine nature at all.
The phrase indicates that the Son was created by God's will to be an object of love.
The phrase means the Son is superabundantly loved by God, not that love caused His generation.
The phrase proves that love is the efficient cause of the Son's existence in the Trinity.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas states that the Apostle calls Christ the 'Son of the love of God' because He is loved superabundantly, not because love was the principle or cause of His generation.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the source of the Son's existence?
options: The Son is created from nothing, just like other creatures.
The Son proceeds from the Father's own substance.
The Son proceeds from a separate essence distinct from the Father.
The Son proceeds from a material source outside the Father.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the Son was not begotten from nothing but from the Father's substance, distinguishing true generation from creation.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the Son must come from the Father's substance?
options: Because the Son must be a true natural son, not a made thing.
Because the Father needs to lose part of his nature to create the Son.
Because the divine nature can be divided into parts for generation.
Because the Son is a creature mentioned in the book of Sirach.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if the Son came from nothing, he would be a 'made' thing rather than a true son; true filiation requires proceeding from the father's own nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas address the objection that the Son is called a 'creature' in Scripture?
options: He argues that the Son is a creature in the same way humans are.
He rejects the verse as inauthentic and not part of the Bible.
He claims the term 'creature' is a metaphor for the Son's divinity.
He says the scriptural 'Wisdom' refers to created wisdom, not the Son.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas explains that the 'Wisdom' described as created in Sirach refers to wisdom given to creatures, not the divine Son.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding power in relation to the internal acts of God?
options: God has no power regarding these acts because they are necessary, not possible.
God possesses the power to generate and breathe forth the other divine persons.
There is no power in God because the divine persons are not made things.
Power exists in God only for external effects, not for internal relations.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that because the Father is the principle of generation and the Father and Son are the principle of spiration, they must possess the corresponding powers to perform these acts.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for attributing this power to God?
options: Power is simply the principle of an act, and the Father is the principle of generation.
Active power must always be distinct from passive power in God.
Intellect and will are separate from power, so power must exist independently.
The divine persons are possible objects, which requires a source of power.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'power' means the principle of an act. Since the Father is the principle of generation, he must have the power of generating.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that power cannot apply to the Son because he proceeds as a word of the intellect?
options: The Son is a passive recipient of power, so he cannot have active power.
The Son proceeds by necessity, so no power is needed for his existence.
Power implies a distinction from its effect, which is only a distinction of reason here.
The intellect is a separate power from the will, so they do not interact.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that power signifies a principle, which implies a distinction. He clarifies that in God, this distinction is one of reason, not a real separation.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about what the 'power of begetting' primarily signifies in God?
options: It signifies both the divine essence and the personal relation equally.
It signifies the personal relation of the Father directly and the essence indirectly.
It signifies the divine essence directly and the relation only indirectly.
It signifies neither the essence nor the relation, but a third concept.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the Son is like the Father in nature, the power to beget must primarily signify that shared divine nature, while the relation is only implied.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying the power of begetting signifies the divine essence?
options: Because the power of begetting is unique to the Father alone.
Because every creator produces something similar to itself in nature.
Because the power to act and the act itself are completely distinct.
Because power is defined as a principle belonging to a specific person.
questions.explanation: Aquinas reasons that since a begetter produces a being like itself in nature, and the Son is like the Father in divine nature, the power must be that nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that 'power' signifies a principle, and thus a relation?
options: Power signifies the relation directly, but the essence is more important.
Power signifies the thing by which an agent acts, not the relation itself.
Power is a genus of relation, so it must signify relation primarily.
Power signifies the agent itself, not the means by which it acts.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas clarifies that power signifies the instrument or means by which an agent acts, rather than the relational aspect of being a principle.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether multiple persons can be the result of a single divine act?
options: Yes, because the Father's power is not reduced after creating the first Son.
No, there is only one Father, one Son, and one Holy Spirit in God.
Yes, but only if the Son chooses not to beget another creator.
No, because the Son lacks the power to beget anyone other than himself.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that in God there is only one Father, one Son, and one Holy Ghost, rejecting the idea of multiple persons from one act.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why there cannot be multiple Sons in God?
options: Divine persons are distinguished by relations, which cannot be multiplied without matter.
The Son is already perfect, so there is no room for another person.
God understands and wills all things through a single, simple act of mind.
Nature is determined to produce only one offspring in any given instance.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since persons are distinct only by their relations (like paternity or filiation), and these relations cannot be multiplied without material distinction (which God lacks), there can only be one of each.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that Augustine said the Son did not beget a Creator because it was not necessary, implying He could have?
options: He states that the Son lacks the power to beget, so necessity is irrelevant.
He agrees that the Son could have begotten another, but chose not to.
He argues that Augustine was mistaken and that the Son actually did beget another.
He clarifies that Augustine meant the Son did not beget, not that He was capable of doing so.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that Augustine's words do not mean the Son *could* beget a Son, but simply that He did not.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether equality exists among the divine persons?
options: Equality must be admitted because inequality would imply different essences.
Equality is accepted only as a metaphor for their shared likeness.
Equality is rejected because the persons are distinct by their relations.
Equality is rejected because it applies only to physical size and bulk.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that we must admit equality because if there were inequality, the persons would not share the same essence, meaning they would not be one God.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for insisting on equality among the divine persons?
options: Inequality would mean they do not share the same divine essence.
Augustine taught that the Father and Son must be equal.
Likeness is insufficient to describe the unity of the Trinity.
Equality is required by the philosophical definition of quantity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that unequal things cannot have the same quantity (essence); therefore, inequality would destroy the unity of God's essence.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that equality implies a relation, but relations distinguish the persons?
options: Equality is not a relation but a property of the essence alone.
The objection is wrong because equality is not reciprocal in God.
Relations are only for created beings, not for divine persons.
Equality implies both distinction of persons and unity of essence.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas states that equality implies both the distinction of persons (since nothing is equal to itself) and the unity of essence.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the timing of the Son's existence?
options: The Son is always in the process of becoming, so He never fully exists yet.
The Son exists eternally, but only because the Father chooses to make Him so.
The Son exists at the exact same time as the Father, with no gap between them.
The Son begins to exist at a specific moment after the Father starts begetting Him.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that the Son is co-eternal with the Father, meaning they exist simultaneously without any temporal delay.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the Son is not later than the Father?
options: The Father uses His free will to choose the exact moment the Son should appear.
Eternity excludes any kind of origin, so the Son cannot have a principle at all.
The Son's nature is perfect from the start, unlike natural agents who mature over time.
The Father's act of begetting is not a step-by-step process that takes time to finish.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the Father's action is not successive (step-by-step) and His nature is perfect from eternity, the effect (the Son) exists simultaneously with the cause.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that anything generated must begin to exist?
options: He says that the objection is wrong because the Son has no principle of origin.
He states that the Son begins to exist but immediately becomes eternal to match the Father.
He claims that the Son is not actually generated, but created by the Father's will.
He argues that divine generation involves no change, so the Son is always being begotten.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that corruption involves change, but divine generation does not; therefore, the Son is ever being begotten without beginning to exist in time.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding an order of nature among the divine persons?
options: There is no order of nature because the divine nature is completely simple and undivided.
There is an order based on origin, but it does not imply that one person is prior to another.
There is an order of essence, meaning one person is fundamentally more essential than the others.
There is a strict hierarchy where the Father is prior to the Son and the Holy Spirit.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while there is an order of origin (one person comes from another), this does not mean one is prior in time or rank, as they are co-equal.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying an order of nature exists in God?
options: Athanasius declared that order is necessary for the Trinity to function as a single God.
Nature implies a beginning in time, which applies to the divine persons as they were created.
Order always refers to a principle, and since there is a principle of origin in God, there must be an order.
The divine essence is complex, requiring an internal structure to distinguish between the different persons.
questions.explanation: Aquinas reasons that order is defined by its reference to a principle; since God has a principle of origin (without temporal priority), an order of nature must exist.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that order implies distinction, but the divine nature has no distinction?
options: He states that the objection is valid, but God's power overrides the logical requirement for distinction in order.
He claims that distinction only exists in created things, so the objection does not apply to God at all.
He clarifies that 'order of nature' refers to the order of origin among persons, not a division within the nature itself.
He argues that the divine nature is actually distinct from the divine essence, allowing for internal ordering.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that the order is about the natural origin of the persons relative to each other, not an ordering or splitting of the divine nature itself.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the relationship between the Son and the Father in terms of greatness?
options: The Son is eternally equal to the Father in greatness.
The Son is equal to the Father only in His human nature.
The Son is greater than the Father due to His divine role.
The Son is less than the Father because He was generated later.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the Son was eternally equal to the Father in greatness, rejecting the idea of inequality based on generation.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for the Son's equality with the Father?
options: The Father’s power to generate was defective, limiting the Son’s growth.
The Son eventually reached equality through a process of gradual change.
The Son shares the Father’s dignity of paternity directly.
The Son possesses the same perfect nature as the Father from the start.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that in God, generation does not involve change or growth from potentiality to act; the Son immediately possesses the full perfection of the divine nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the Father is greater because He is subject to no one?
options: He says this applies only to Christ’s human nature, not His divine nature.
He claims the Father’s greatness comes from being the universal whole.
He states that the Son’s subjection is a sign of His higher status.
He argues that the Son is also subject to the Father in divinity.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas clarifies that the scriptures cited refer to Christ's human nature, where He is subject, while in His divine nature He is equal.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the Son is in the Father, and vice versa?
options: They are only in each other metaphorically, not in any real or literal sense.
The Son is in the Father, but the Father is not in the Son because He is the source.
They are distinct persons and therefore cannot exist within one another at all.
They are mutually contained in each other through their shared essence, relations, and origin.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that according to essence, relation, and origin, the Son and Father are in each other.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for the Father being in the Son?
options: The Father and Son are the same person, so one is naturally inside the other.
The Son is a part of the Father's substance that was separated from Him.
The Father shares His divine nature with the Son without changing or leaving Himself.
The Father's power extends over the Son, keeping Him contained within His will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the Father is His own essence and communicates this essence to the Son without change, the Father Himself is in the Son.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the Son came 'out' of the Father and thus cannot be 'in' Him?
options: The Father is so large that He can contain everything that comes from Him.
The Son returned to the Father immediately after coming out, so He is now inside.
The Son's origin is like a word forming in the mind, remaining inside the thinker.
The Son did not actually come out, but only appeared to do so for our benefit.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas compares the Son's procession to a word emerging from the heart yet remaining within it, denying any essential separation.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the power of the Son compared to the Father?
options: The Son is equal to the Father in power.
The Son's power is different in kind, so they cannot be compared.
The Son has less power because he acts only by seeing the Father act.
The Son has greater power because he obeys the Father's commands.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that the Son is necessarily equal to the Father in power.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the Son must be equal to the Father in power?
options: The Father commands the Son to act, which implies a hierarchy of power.
The Son receives his essence from the Father, making him a lesser being.
The Son cannot beget another son, which limits his specific divine abilities.
Power follows from the perfection of nature, and the Son shares the Father's nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that power is a consequence of perfection in nature, and since the Son is equal to the Father in nature, he is equal in power.

questions.q: How does Aquinas explain the objection that the Father 'teaches' and 'commands' the Son?
options: It proves the Son is a subordinate servant who must follow instructions.
It shows the Father is the source of the Son's knowledge and will through begetting.
It indicates that the Son learns new things from the Father over time.
It means the Father has authority to restrict the Son's independent actions.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that 'showing' and 'commanding' refer to the Father communicating knowledge and will to the Son through the eternal act of begetting, not to a temporal hierarchy.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether a divine person can be sent?
options: It is a misunderstanding of language and should not be used.
It is impossible because divine persons are never inferior to one another.
It is only possible if the divine person physically leaves heaven.
It is a fitting and proper thing for a divine person to be sent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the mission of a divine person is a 'fitting thing,' rejecting the objections that it implies inferiority or physical separation.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what two elements define the concept of 'mission' for a divine person?
options: The origin from the sender and a new way of existing in a place.
Physical movement from one location to another and obedience.
Separation from the sender and arrival at a new destination.
The sender's command and the receiver's inferior status.
questions.explanation: Aquinas defines mission as involving the procession of origin from the sender and a new mode of presence, such as the Son becoming visible in the world through taking human nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the sent must be inferior to the sender?
options: Inferiority applies only when sent by command or counsel, not by origin.
Inferiority is irrelevant because divine persons do not interact.
The objection is wrong because the sender is always the servant.
Divine persons are indeed unequal, but this does not affect their mission.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that mission implies inferiority only when it involves command or counsel, where the commander is greater; this does not apply to the eternal procession of divine persons by origin.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the mission of a divine person is eternal or temporal?
options: Mission is both eternal and temporal because it includes the eternal procession.
Mission is only temporal because it involves a divine person being in a creature.
Mission is neither eternal nor temporal because divine persons do not change.
Mission is exclusively eternal because it mirrors the eternal birth of the Son.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that 'mission' has only a temporal significance in God because it implies a divine person existing in or being possessed by a creature, which is a new, time-bound event.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for distinguishing 'mission' from 'generation'?
options: Generation is a visible act, whereas mission is an invisible act of the spirit.
Mission implies a new, time-bound presence in a creature, while generation is eternal.
Generation refers to a new, time-bound state, while mission refers to an eternal state.
Mission involves a change in the divine person, while generation does not involve change.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that 'generation' expresses an eternal term, whereas 'mission' expresses a temporal term because it involves a divine person being in something else (a creature) in a new mode.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that mission must be eternal because a divine person cannot be changed?
options: He states that the objection is invalid because mission does not imply any change.
He argues that the change occurs in the creature, not in the divine person.
He agrees that the divine person changes, but this change is eternal in nature.
He claims that divine persons are changed only when they become human beings.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas clarifies that the temporal aspect of mission comes from a change in the creature (who newly possesses or receives the divine person), not from any change in the divine person themselves.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding how a divine person is invisibly sent to a human soul?
options: It happens whenever God is present in creation.
It happens when the divine person is known by faith.
It happens only through the gift of sanctifying grace.
It happens through any gift of grace, including miracles.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the invisible mission and temporal proceeding of the divine person occur only according to sanctifying grace, rejecting the idea that other graces suffice for this specific indwelling.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that sanctifying grace is the only basis for this invisible mission?
options: Because it allows us to freely enjoy and possess the divine person.
Because it is the only grace that gives us knowledge of God.
Because it is the only grace that enables us to perform miracles.
Because it is the only way God can be present in the world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that we possess only what we can freely use or enjoy, and sanctifying grace is the specific gift that enables the soul to enjoy the divine person, thus constituting the mission.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the Holy Spirit was given for miracles (Objection 4)?
options: Miracles prove that the Spirit is sent without grace.
Miracles are manifestations that point to sanctifying grace.
The objection is wrong because miracles do not come from God.
Miracles are a separate form of sanctifying grace.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 4, Aquinas clarifies that miraculous gifts are 'manifestations of the Spirit' that reveal sanctifying grace, rather than being the basis for the invisible mission themselves.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the Father can be described as being sent?
options: The Father is sent only when grace indwells the human soul.
The Father is sent because He freely gives Himself to creatures.
The Father is sent in the same way as the Son and the Holy Spirit.
The Father is not sent because He does not originate from another person.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the Father cannot be fittingly called 'sent' because the concept of mission requires originating from another, which does not apply to the Father.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why the Father is not sent?
options: The term 'mission' implies a procession from another, which the Father lacks.
The Father is not a distinct person within the Trinity.
The Father lacks the authority to bestow grace upon believers.
The Father does not dwell in humans through the gift of grace.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'mission' means coming from another, and since the Father is not from another, He cannot be sent.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the Father gives Himself, so He should be called sent?
options: He denies that the Father gives Himself in any sense to creatures.
He claims the objection is invalid because the Father is not a giver.
He agrees that the Father is sent because giving implies being sent.
He says 'giving' as a free bestowal applies to the Father, but 'being sent' does not.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas distinguishes between freely giving oneself (which the Father does) and being sent (which implies originating from another).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the Son is sent invisibly?
options: Yes, the Son is sent invisibly because He dwells in the soul by grace and originates from another.
No, only the Holy Spirit is sent invisibly because all gifts of grace belong to Him.
Yes, but only when the person receiving Him has perfect knowledge of all mysteries.
No, the Son is never sent, but only the Father and the Holy Spirit are sent.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since the Son dwells in the soul by grace and proceeds from another, it is fitting for Him to be sent invisibly, just like the Holy Spirit.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the Son can be sent invisibly?
options: Invisible sending requires the person to dwell in the soul by grace and to have an origin from another.
Invisible sending is possible only if the person is the first Gift, which is Love.
Invisible sending is fitting because the Son is distinct from the Father in substance.
Invisible sending requires the person to possess all intellectual gifts, such as prophecy and knowledge.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that invisible mission signifies both a new indwelling by grace and an origin from another, conditions met by both the Son and the Holy Spirit.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that only the Holy Spirit is sent because all gifts belong to Him?
options: The objection is wrong because the Son is not sent at all, only the Holy Spirit is sent.
The objection fails because the gifts of grace are actually given by the Father, not the Spirit.
The objection is invalid because the Son and the Holy Spirit are the same person.
While all gifts are attributed to the Spirit as Love, some gifts are specifically appropriated to the Son.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 1, Aquinas clarifies that although the Spirit is the first Gift, certain gifts are appropriated to the Son by their nature.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the invisible mission?
options: It is sent to everyone who has grace and experiences a renewal through it.
It is sent only to those who are making continuous progress in virtue.
It is not sent to the Old Testament Fathers because the Spirit was not yet given.
It is sent only to those who are not yet perfectly united to God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that the invisible mission is sent to all in whom two conditions are found: the indwelling of grace and a certain renewal by grace.

questions.q: What are the two conditions Aquinas says must be present for the invisible mission to be sent?
options: The person must possess grace and experience a renewal through that grace.
The person must be in the Old Testament and must not have fullness of grace.
The person must be a creature and must be in a state of distance from God.
The person must be receiving sacraments and must be an instrument of grace.
questions.explanation: In his answer, Aquinas states that the invisible mission implies the indwelling of grace and a certain renewal by grace.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that the invisible mission is not sent to Christ or the blessed because they are perfectly united to God?
options: He claims that the mission is sent to them continuously as their grace increases in intensity.
He states that the mission is not sent to them at all because they are too close to God.
He argues that they are sent the mission only at the very start of their beatitude.
He explains that the mission is sent to them only after the day of judgment.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas states that the invisible mission is directed to the blessed at the very beginning of their beatitude.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the visible sending of the Holy Ghost?
options: It is fitting because humans need visible signs to understand invisible spiritual realities.
It is unnecessary because the Holy Ghost is already present in all visible creatures.
It is unfitting because the Holy Ghost is never described as being less than the Father.
It is fitting only if the Holy Ghost assumes a human nature like the Son did.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because human nature requires learning about invisible things through visible ones, it was appropriate for the Holy Ghost to be sent in a visible manner.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the specific role of the visible mission of the Holy Ghost?
options: To serve as a visible sign that points to the gift of sanctification.
To act as the author who directly creates sanctification in believers.
To demonstrate that the Holy Ghost is superior to the Son in power.
To replace the need for the invisible mission of the Holy Ghost.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes the roles, stating the Son is sent as the author of sanctification, while the Holy Ghost is sent as the sign of that sanctification.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that angels, not the Holy Ghost, are the ones sent visibly?
options: He argues that the visible creatures were formed by angels to signify the Holy Ghost.
He agrees that the angels are the primary agents of the visible mission.
He claims that the Holy Ghost assumed the visible creatures into His own person.
He states that visible appearances are impossible because they belong only to prophecy.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fifth objection, Aquinas explains that while angels formed the visible creatures, they did so to signify the Person of the Holy Ghost, not themselves.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who sends a divine person?
options: The entire Trinity, because all three persons cause the effect of the mission.
Only the specific person from whom the sent one eternally proceeds.
Only the Father, since He is the ultimate source of all divinity.
The person being sent, acting independently of the others.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the sent person proceeds from a specific principle, the act of sending involves the effect of the mission, which is caused by the whole Trinity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying the whole Trinity sends?
options: Because human beings can also participate in sending the Holy Spirit.
Because the sender is defined by causing the visible or invisible effect of the mission.
Because authority over the sent person belongs equally to all three divine persons.
Because Augustine explicitly stated that the Son sends Himself alone.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes between the principle of origin (which is specific) and the principle of the effect (which belongs to the whole Trinity), concluding the latter defines 'sending'.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a man could send the Holy Ghost?
options: He agrees that men can send the Spirit through the power of grace.
He claims the Holy Ghost is never sent by anyone.
He argues that only the Father has the authority to send.
He rejects it because men cannot cause the effect of grace.
questions.explanation: Aquinas refutes the idea that a man can send the Holy Ghost by stating that humans lack the power to cause the effect of grace, which is required for sending.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the origin of all existing things?
options: Some beings exist without a cause, just like a person can lack whiteness.
Only necessary things are created by God; others exist on their own.
Mathematical objects prove that not all beings need an efficient cause.
Every existing thing is caused by God as its source of being.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'every being in any way existing is from God' because all beings participate in being, which must be caused by the one who possesses being essentially.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why all things must come from God?
options: Necessary things do not require causes, so God is the cause of contingent things only.
God is the only being that possesses existence essentially, while others only borrow it.
Plato argued that unity must come before multitude in all physical objects.
God is the greatest in heat, so He causes all other forms of warmth.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that God is 'essentially self-subsisting Being,' whereas all other beings exist by 'participation,' meaning they do not have being in themselves but receive it from God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that mathematical proofs do not use efficient causes?
options: The objection is wrong because all sciences must use the same type of cause.
Mathematics deals with mentally abstracted objects, not real things that need physical causes.
God is the cause of mathematical truths, but not of the physical objects they describe.
Mathematical proofs are invalid because they do not follow Aristotle's rules of logic.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that mathematics treats objects as 'abstracted mentally,' whereas in reality, everything has an efficient cause in proportion to its being.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether primary matter is created by God?
options: Primary matter is eternal and was never created by any cause.
Primary matter is created by God, the universal cause of all being.
Primary matter exists independently of God as a separate first principle.
Primary matter creates itself through natural processes like condensation.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God is the cause of things as beings, He must cause not just their forms but also the underlying matter itself.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God must create primary matter?
options: Matter is purely potential and therefore cannot exist without being acted upon by a purely actual being.
Ancient philosophers failed to understand that matter is actually a form of divine energy.
God is the cause of existence itself, so He must cause everything that contributes to a thing's being, including matter.
Matter is the passive counterpart to God's active power, so they must be two equal, uncreated principles.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the cause of things considered as 'beings' must be the cause of all aspects of their being, which includes primary matter.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God and matter are opposing principles, neither from the other?
options: He suggests that passion and action are identical, so the distinction between God and matter is false.
He claims that matter is actually active, not passive, so it is similar to God in nature.
He argues that the first passive principle (matter) is the effect of the first active principle (God).
He states that God and matter are indeed two separate, uncreated principles that oppose each other.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that since every imperfect thing is caused by a perfect one, the first passive principle is caused by the first active principle.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the source of the perfect models for all created things?
options: God is the only first source of these models for everything.
Nature creates its own models without any divine input.
Separate, self-existing species exist independently of God.
The models are found in the minds of human scientists.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that God is the first exemplar cause of all things and that the types of all things exist in the divine wisdom.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the divine mind must be the source of these models?
options: Because human minds are too weak to design complex forms.
To ensure created things receive specific and distinct forms.
Because the Bible explicitly lists the designs for every animal.
Because God is physically similar to the creatures he makes.
questions.explanation: He argues that an exemplar is needed so the effect can receive a determinate form, and this determination is reduced to divine wisdom.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creatures are too different from God to be like Him?
options: Creatures are like God because they have the same physical shape.
Creatures are like God because they reflect the ideas in His mind.
Creatures are like God because they share the same biological species.
Creatures are like God because they possess independent self-existence.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas compares a material house to the house in an architect's mind, stating creatures represent the divine idea.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God is the final cause of all things?
options: No, because acting for an end implies a need that God does not possess.
No, God acts only as an efficient cause, not as a final cause for creation.
Yes, but only for intelligent beings who consciously choose to desire God.
Yes, God is the final cause because His goodness is the goal all creatures seek.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that divine goodness is the end of all things, meaning God is the final cause because creatures seek to acquire perfection which is a likeness of His goodness.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the main reason God acts as the First Agent?
options: To ensure that primary matter exists, which is the true first principle of reality.
To satisfy a natural need, as all agents must act to achieve a missing end.
To communicate His perfection and goodness to others, not to gain anything for Himself.
To acquire the form of the things He generates, completing His own nature.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the First Agent acts only to communicate His perfection (goodness), unlike imperfect agents who act to acquire something they lack.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God cannot be the final cause because acting for an end implies need?
options: The objection is valid for God, so He is not the final cause of inanimate objects.
God acts for an end only when He creates intelligent beings who can recognize Him.
God has a need to create, but it is a spiritual need rather than a physical one.
Acting from need applies only to imperfect agents; God acts freely to share His goodness.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 1, Aquinas states that acting from need belongs to imperfect agents who are both agent and patient, whereas God acts only for His own goodness.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the definition of creation?
options: Creation means making something new out of pre-existing materials.
Creation is the bringing forth of all being from absolute nothingness.
Creation involves improving existing things to a higher state.
Creation is a process that requires a material cause to start.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that creation is the emanation of all being from a universal cause, meaning it proceeds from 'nothing' (no being) rather than from any pre-existing matter.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why creation comes from nothing?
options: Because God is too powerful to rely on any physical materials.
Because no being could exist before the first universal cause.
Because Augustine explicitly defined creation as starting from zero.
Because 'nothing' is a more noble starting point than matter.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since creation is the origin of all being from the first principle, it is impossible for any being to have existed before this emanation.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that 'from' implies a material cause?
options: He says the preposition 'from' here indicates sequence, not material origin.
He states that the objection misunderstands the definition of a statue.
He argues that 'nothing' can act as a material cause in this case.
He claims that material causes are irrelevant to the act of creation.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that the preposition 'from' in this context signifies order or sequence (like morning coming before midday), not a material source.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether God can create anything?
options: It is necessary to say that God created all things from nothing.
Creation is impossible because there is an infinite distance between being and nothing.
God cannot create because ancient philosophers proved nothing comes from nothing.
God can create, but only by shaping pre-existing natural materials.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is not only possible but necessary to affirm that all things were created by God from nothing.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for concluding that God must create from nothing?
options: Because change always requires a subject, and nothing exists before creation.
Because if God used pre-existing matter, that matter would not be caused by Him.
Because ancient philosophers were wrong about the nature of movement and time.
Because God is a craftsman who needs raw materials like wood to work with.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that if God acted on something already existing, that thing would not be caused by Him; since God is the cause of all being, He must bring things into existence from nothing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creation involves crossing an infinite distance between being and nothing?
options: He argues that there is no infinite medium between nothing and being.
He claims that being and nothing are actually the same thing in different forms.
He states that creation is a slow process that takes an infinite amount of time.
He agrees that the distance is infinite, but God's power is stronger than distance.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas rejects the idea of an infinite medium between nothing and being, calling it a false imagination derived from viewing creation as a change between forms.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about the nature of creation within the created thing?
options: It is a real physical substance added to the creature.
It is a medium that exists separately between God and the creature.
It is a real relation connecting the creature to its Creator.
It is a temporary accident that changes the creature's essence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that creation places something in the thing created according to relation only, specifically a real relation to the Creator as the principle of its being.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that creation is only a relation and not a change?
options: Because there is no medium between the Creator and the creature.
Because the creature is the subject of the creation process.
Because God creates without movement, leaving only relation when motion is removed.
Because creatures are made from pre-existing material through movement.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that creation is not made by movement or change because it does not come from something pre-existing; when movement is removed, only relation remains.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creation cannot be a medium between God and the creature?
options: He says creation is a medium only in the active sense, not the passive.
He agrees that creation is not a medium and rejects the term entirely.
He claims the creature is the medium, not the act of creation.
He argues that since creation signifies change, it acts as a medium between them.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas states that because creation is signified as a change, and change is a kind of medium, creation is also signified as a medium.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, who or what are properly called 'created things'?
options: Matter alone, since it is the underlying substrate of all physical objects.
Abstract concepts like 'being' itself, rather than individual objects.
Only things that exist as independent, complete entities in their own right.
Forms and accidents, because they are the principles that make things be.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'being' properly belongs to subsisting things (independent entities), so only these are truly 'created,' whereas forms and accidents are merely 'concreated.'

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying creation belongs to subsisting things?
options: Natural generation produces matter, which is the primary component of creation.
Composite things are more complex than simple things, requiring more divine power.
Creation is a form of making, and making aims at the being of a thing.
The book De Causis states that the first creature is being itself.
questions.explanation: He reasons that to be created is to be made, and making is directed toward a thing's being, which properly belongs only to things that subsist (exist independently).

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that composite things are not created because they come from parts?
options: Creation refers only to the addition of a new form to pre-existing matter.
The objection is correct; only simple, non-composite substances are truly created.
Creation brings the whole composite into being simultaneously with all its parts.
Composite things are not created, but only their individual parts are created separately.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that creation is not building from pre-existing parts, but bringing the entire composite entity into existence along with all its principles.

questions.q: What is Aquinas’s final conclusion regarding who can create?
options: God creates alone, but He can give creatures the power to create indirectly.
Only God can create, and no creature can do so even with God's help.
Perfect creatures can create because they can make things like themselves.
Any being with enough power can create since created things are finite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that it is impossible for any creature to create, either by its own power or instrumentally, because creation is the proper act of God alone.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why only God can create?
options: Material things cannot create because they need to touch or move existing matter.
Creation brings existence into being from nothing, which is the most universal effect.
God is the only being that is infinite, so only He can make finite things.
Creating from nothing requires more power than making something from its opposite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that 'being itself' is the most universal effect, and therefore it must come from the most universal cause, which is God.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that creating from nothing is easier than changing existing matter?
options: He states that the contrary resists less than nothing, making creation simpler.
He argues that nothing resists the creator, so no special power is actually needed.
He claims that finite effects always require finite power, regardless of the source.
He says the power needed depends on the mode of being made, not just the result.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the second objection, Aquinas explains that the maker's power is measured by the mode of production; creating from nothing shows infinite power even if the effect is finite.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, is the act of creating something unique to one specific Person of the Trinity, or is it shared?
options: It is unique to the Holy Spirit alone.
It is unique to the Son alone.
It is common to the entire Trinity.
It is unique to the Father alone.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creating belongs to God's essence, which is shared by all three Persons, so it is common to the whole Trinity.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for saying creation is not proper to just one Person?
options: Because creation flows from God's essence, which is shared by all three Persons.
Because the Father creates independently of the Son and Holy Spirit.
Because creation is an accidental property rather than an essential one.
Because the divine Persons are too similar to have distinct creative roles.
questions.explanation: He states that since every agent produces its like, the principle of action is the agent's being (essence), which is common to the three Persons.

questions.q: In his reply to Objection 2, how does Aquinas explain the order among the Persons regarding creation?
options: The Father creates first, then the Son, and finally the Holy Spirit acts last.
The Holy Spirit is the primary cause, with the Father and Son assisting.
There is no order because all three Persons act simultaneously and identically.
The Son receives nature from the Father, and the Spirit from both, establishing an order.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that while the power is common, it belongs to them in an order: the Son receives from the Father, and the Spirit from both.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether creatures bear a trace of the Trinity?
options: Only rational creatures bear a trace of the Trinity.
Every creature necessarily bears a trace of the Trinity.
No creature bears a trace because the Trinity is invisible.
Creatures bear an image, but never a trace, of the Trinity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that while rational creatures have an 'image' of the Trinity, 'in all creatures there is found the trace of the Trinity.'

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that every creature contains a trace of the Trinity?
options: Because smoke represents fire, and all creatures are effects of God.
Because every creature possesses intellect and will, mirroring the Son and Holy Spirit.
Because the Trinity directly creates only rational beings, not irrational ones.
Because every creature has substance, form, and order, which reflect the divine persons.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that substance reflects the Father, form reflects the Son (Word), and order/relation reflects the Holy Spirit (Love), constituting the trace in all creatures.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that finding a trace in every property leads to an infinite regress?
options: The trace is found only in the will, which is not divisible.
The trace applies only to the creature as a whole, not to every part.
Properties do not exist in creatures, so they cannot have traces.
The infinite regress is acceptable because God is infinite in nature.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas clarifies that a creature is a 'self-subsisting thing' and the trace is ascribed to the whole being, not to every individual property within it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between creation and natural processes?
options: Creation happens simultaneously with every act of nature and art.
Nature creates the forms directly without any prior divine action.
Creation is a prerequisite that exists before nature begins its work.
Creation and nature are two separate, unconnected processes.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creation does not enter into the work of nature but is presupposed to it, meaning it must happen first.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why nature does not create forms directly?
options: Forms are too powerful to be produced by natural agents.
Matter is too unstable to hold any form in place.
Natural agents lack the power to produce anything from nothing.
Forms are not independent things, so they cannot be made or created.
questions.explanation: He states that forms do not exist on their own; therefore, they are not 'made' or 'created' but are 'concreated' with the composite thing.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that nature's products must be creatures or it is heretical?
options: Heretics are wrong to claim that nature's products are not creatures.
Nature's products are created directly by God, bypassing natural causes.
Nature's products are creatures because they rely on already-created principles.
Nature's products are not creatures, so the objection is invalid.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, he explains that nature operates only on the assumption of created principles, making its products creatures.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's conclusion regarding whether the universe always existed?
options: It is impossible to prove by reason that the universe had a beginning.
The universe must have always existed because God is eternal.
The universe definitely began to exist at a specific moment in time.
The universe exists eternally because it is incorruptible.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that while the world began to exist by God's will, this fact cannot be demonstrated by reason alone; it is an article of faith.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas believe we cannot prove by reason that the world had a beginning?
options: Aristotle proved that the world is eternal, and Aquinas agrees with him.
Human reason is too weak to understand the concept of time.
God's will is free, so He did not have to will the world to exist eternally.
The world is necessary because God is the sufficient cause of all things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that since God's will is not necessitated to will anything except Himself, it is not necessary for the world to be eternal, making its beginning a matter of divine choice, not logical necessity.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that a beginning of the world implies a 'vacuum' (empty space) existed before it?
options: He states that a vacuum is possible if it is caused by God's power.
He agrees that a vacuum existed but says it was not empty of God.
He argues that space and place did not exist before the world was created.
He claims that God filled the vacuum with spiritual beings before creating matter.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that 'vacuum' implies a space capable of holding a body; since there was no place or space before the world, there was no vacuum.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether the world had a beginning?
options: It is a matter of personal opinion that varies depending on the philosopher's view.
It is a fact that can be proven with absolute certainty using logical reasoning alone.
It is a truth known only through faith, not through human demonstration or science.
It is a philosophical error because the world must have existed from all eternity.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the newness of the world is held by faith alone and cannot be proved by any demonstration.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the world's beginning cannot be proven by reason?
options: The world is too old for any human to have witnessed its actual creation.
The essence of things is universal and does not include specific limits of time or place.
Logical arguments are only useful for proving things that happen in the present moment.
God's will is too complex for human minds to understand or investigate in any way.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the essence of a thing is abstracted from 'here' and 'now', it cannot be demonstrated that a specific thing did not always exist.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that an eternal world would mean an infinite number of days passed before today?
options: He states that time is an illusion and therefore the concept of passing days is invalid.
He argues that between any specific past day and today, the number of days is finite.
He claims that days did not exist until God created the sun and moon recently.
He agrees that an infinite number of days makes the existence of the world impossible.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 6, Aquinas explains that passage is from term to term, and between any chosen past day and the present, there is only a finite number of days.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding when God created the world?
options: Creation occurred before time began to exist.
The world has existed forever and has no beginning.
Creation happened at the very start of time, not before it.
Time was created separately after the physical world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that 'In the beginning' refers to the beginning of time, meaning heaven and earth were created together with time itself.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that creation happened at the beginning of time?
options: Because time, matter, and spiritual beings were all created simultaneously.
Because the physical world existed before time started flowing.
Because God needed time to measure the process of making things.
Because evil things were created before good things in time.
questions.explanation: He states that four things—corporeal matter, the highest heaven, time, and angelic nature—were created together, so creation coincides with time's start.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that creation implies a 'before' and 'after' which cannot exist at time's indivisible start?
options: Creation is not a movement with duration, so it does not require a 'before' and 'after'.
The 'before' and 'after' refer to God's eternal plan, not physical time.
Creation happened slowly over a long period before time began.
Time is divisible, so the beginning of time actually contains many moments.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas clarifies that the Philosopher's rule about 'before' and 'after' applies to movement, but creation is not a movement.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, where does the variety and difference of things in the universe ultimately originate?
options: From the deliberate intention of God.
From the random movement of matter alone.
From the inherent nature of matter seeking form.
From secondary spiritual beings created by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas rejects the ideas that matter or secondary agents cause diversity, concluding instead that it comes from God's intention.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for rejecting the idea that secondary agents (like first intelligences) cause the diversity of things?
options: Because secondary agents are too simple to understand complexity.
Because only God has the power to create being from nothing.
Because matter prevents secondary agents from acting effectively.
Because God forbids secondary agents from creating anything.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that creation belongs to God alone, and since diverse things require creation, they must come from Him, not secondary causes.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that God, being one, must produce only one effect?
options: The one effect is so large it appears as many.
God produces one effect that then splits into many.
God is actually many things disguised as one.
God acts by will and intellect, allowing for multiple effects.
questions.explanation: Aquinas distinguishes God as a voluntary agent acting by intellect, unlike natural agents that act by a single fixed form.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether inequality in the world comes from God?
options: Inequality exists because God is just and must give unequal things to unequal beings.
Inequality is not from God but resulted from the free choices of rational creatures.
God created all things equal initially, and inequality arose later due to sin.
God’s wisdom is the direct cause of the inequality found among different kinds of things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that just as God's wisdom causes the distinction of things, it is also the cause of their inequality, rejecting the idea that it stems from sin or free will.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why God creates a hierarchy of different kinds of things?
options: Because it is necessary to show that God is the best agent by making the best parts.
To punish souls that turned away from God, resulting in the creation of bodies.
Because different forms require different levels of perfection to arrange species in degrees.
Because God is one, and unity naturally leads to the creation of equal things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that formal distinctions (different species) require inequality because forms vary like numbers, creating a natural arrangement where some species are more perfect than others.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that the best agent should make all parts equally best?
options: He agrees that God should make all things equal to reflect divine unity.
He argues that the whole is best if parts are unequal, like an eye in an animal.
He states that equality is the first effect of unity, so God must start with equality.
He claims that inequality is only relevant for rewards, not for the creation of things.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the first objection, Aquinas explains that a whole is best when its parts are proportioned to it, not when every part has the same dignity, using the example of an animal's eye.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the number of worlds?
options: There is only one single world.
The number of worlds is unknown.
God could create many worlds but chose not to.
There are many worlds created by God.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly concludes that the order of created things shows there is only one world, rejecting the idea of multiple worlds.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's main reason for believing there is only one world?
options: Matter can only exist in one specific location.
All created things are ordered together into a single unified system.
God's power is limited to creating only one universe.
Creating many worlds would be too wasteful of resources.
questions.explanation: He argues that because all things come from God, they relate to each other and to God in a single order, forming one world.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that 'many good things are better than a few'?
options: He argues that an endless number lacks a definite goal or end.
He states that other worlds would physically collide with ours.
He says that nature cannot produce more than one world.
