He claims that God prefers quality over quantity in creation.
questions.explanation: In Reply 2, Aquinas states that material plurality tends toward infinity, and since infinity opposes the notion of a definite end, God does not intend it.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil is a nature?
options: Evil is a positive force that exists alongside good.
Evil is a distinct genus, separate from being and goodness.
Evil is a nature, but only in the realm of moral actions.
Evil is not a nature; it is simply the absence of good.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that evil signifies the absence of good and is neither a being nor a nature.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for saying evil is not a nature?
options: Because every nature seeks its own being, and being is inherently good.
Because Aristotle claimed that evil is merely a logical category.
Because evil cannot act on its own to corrupt good things.
Because the universe would be imperfect if evil were a real nature.
questions.explanation: He argues that since every nature desires its own being and perfection, and being is good, evil cannot signify being or any nature.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that evil acts (by corrupting good) and therefore must be a being?
options: He argues that corruption is not a true action in the philosophical sense.
He admits evil acts but says it is a weak form of being.
He says evil acts formally as a lack, like whiteness makes things white.
He claims evil only acts when joined to a good nature.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 4, Aquinas explains that evil acts 'formally' as a privation or corruption of good, similar to how whiteness acts to make something white.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil exists in created things?
options: Evil is a positive substance that exists alongside good things in the universe.
Evil is found in things, specifically as a failure or lack of expected goodness.
Evil does not exist because God always creates only the best possible things.
Evil is not found in things because it is too distant from existence to be real.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that evil is found in things as a 'privation,' meaning it is the failure of a thing to possess the goodness it ought to have, rather than a positive entity.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why evil must exist in the universe?
options: God made evil to punish humans for their disobedience and moral failures.
Evil is necessary to balance out the good, ensuring that neither side dominates.
The universe is more perfect if it includes a range of beings, some of which can fail or corrupt.
Nature is imperfect and therefore inevitably produces evil alongside good things.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that the perfection of the universe requires inequality and variety, including corruptible beings that can fail in goodness, which allows for the full realization of all grades of goodness.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that God always makes the best, so there should be no evil?
options: God makes the best whole universe, which includes some parts that can fail for the greater good.
God makes the best in every single part, but evil arises from human misuse.
God allows evil because He is distant from existence and cannot control all things.
God does not make everything; nature makes the imperfect parts where evil is found.
questions.explanation: In his reply to Objection 3, Aquinas states that God makes what is best for the whole universe, not necessarily for every single part, and the whole is better if some parts can fail.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil exists within good?
options: Evil is completely separate from good and has no connection to it whatsoever.
Evil is a positive substance that exists independently of any good thing.
Good and evil are identical, so they cannot be distinguished from one another.
Evil is found within good, because good serves as the underlying subject for evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that evil is in good as its subject because evil is a lack of good in something that is capable of having it.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas argue that the subject of evil must be good?
options: Because evil is a missing quality in something that exists, and all existing things are good.
Because good and evil are opposites that must always be found together in nature.
Because evil is a physical substance that needs a physical container to exist.
Because good is the only thing powerful enough to contain and control evil effectively.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since every actual being is good, and evil is a lack in a being, the thing lacking the good (the subject) must itself be good.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that evil cannot be in good because they are opposites?
options: The rule about opposites does not apply to spiritual matters like good and evil.
Evil is in a good subject, but not in the specific good that is missing.
The objection is wrong because evil is not a real thing, so it has no subject.
Good and evil are not actually opposites, but rather different types of existence.
questions.explanation: Aquinas clarifies that while evil is in a good subject (like an animal), it is not in the specific good it lacks (like sight).

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil completely destroys good?
options: Evil always destroys the entire good because good and evil are direct opposites.
Evil destroys the good entirely, leaving nothing behind in the subject.
Evil can never completely consume good, though it may diminish some aspects of it.
Evil consumes good only if the good is infinite, which created goods are not.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that 'Evil cannot wholly consume good,' distinguishing between goods that are destroyed, those that remain, and those that are merely diminished.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why evil does not destroy all good?
options: He distinguishes between different types of good, noting that the underlying subject always remains.
He claims that evil is not a real thing, but merely the absence of good.
He asserts that good is uniform and indivisible, so it cannot be partially removed.
He argues that good is infinite and therefore cannot be exhausted by finite evil.
questions.explanation: Aquinas categorizes good into three kinds, emphasizing that while some good is destroyed, the 'subject' of evil (the underlying substance) always remains intact.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that good is uniform and thus wholly taken away by evil?
options: The objection is wrong because evil does not actually take away good, it only hides it.
Good relates to different things; it is diminished where it touches action but remains where it touches the subject.
Good is infinite, so even if it is uniform, it can never be fully consumed by evil.
Good is not uniform; it is composed of many separate parts that evil can only remove one by one.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 2, Aquinas explains that good is a medium between subject and act; it is diminished regarding the act but remains regarding the subject.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding whether evil is adequately divided into pain and fault?
options: The division is adequate, but only for evils found in beings with free will.
The division is superfluous because all evil is essentially just pain.
The division is incorrect because temptation is a third category of evil.
The division is inadequate because it ignores defects in non-living things like stones.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that pain and fault adequately cover all evil in 'voluntary things' (rational creatures with will), but do not apply to irrational creatures or mere natural defects.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas claim that evil in rational creatures takes the form of either pain or fault?
options: Because rational creatures are more complex than stones, so they suffer more physical damage.
Because God punishes rational creatures more severely than irrational ones for their defects.
Because rational creatures can feel temptation, which is distinct from both pain and fault.
Because rational creatures have a will, so losing their natural integrity feels like pain against their will.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that because good is the object of the will, the loss of natural integrity (form) is against the will (pain), and the failure of voluntary action is a fault.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that temptation is an evil that is neither pain nor fault?
options: He says temptation is not an evil at all, but merely an opportunity to practice virtue.
He argues that for the tempter, temptation is a fault, and for the tempted, it is not a fault unless they consent.
He asserts that temptation is a pain for the tempter and a fault for the person being tempted.
He claims temptation is a pain because it causes anxiety before the sin occurs.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that temptation is a fault for the one tempting, but not a fault for the one tempted unless they change internally (consent).

questions.q: According to Aquinas, which is the greater evil: fault (moral wrong) or pain (suffering)?
options: They are equal evils since both involve a lack of good.
Pain is worse because it deprives us of God's vision.
Fault is the greater evil because it corrupts the will.
Pain is the greater evil because it harms the person directly.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that fault is worse because it involves a disordered act of the will, which is the source of moral evil, whereas pain is merely a privation of goods.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming that fault is worse than pain?
options: Fault opposes the good of action, while pain opposes the agent.
Fault makes a person evil, while pain does not make a person evil.
Pain is only physical, while fault affects the soul permanently.
God causes pain as punishment, but never causes moral fault.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that one becomes evil through the evil of fault (a bad will), but being punished or suffering pain does not make a person evil in themselves.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that fault is like merit and pain is like reward?
options: He states that merit and fault are unrelated concepts.
He says merit is actually worse than reward, so fault is worse.
He argues that pain is intended to help us avoid fault.
He claims that reward is not truly good for the agent.
questions.explanation: In Reply 1, Aquinas explains that unlike merit which aims at reward, fault is not intended for pain; rather, pain is brought about so that fault may be avoided.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether the soul is a body?
options: The soul is both a body and an incorporeal principle.
The soul is not a body, but the act of a body.
The soul is a body that moves other bodies.
The soul is a body that also has a separate incorporeal part.
questions.explanation: Aquinas says the soul is not a body but the act of a body.

questions.q: What main reason does Aquinas give for the soul not being a body?
options: The soul is a body because it is the only thing that can give life to bodies.
The soul is a body because it is the moving principle of the body.
The soul must be a body because it moves the body.
A body cannot be the first principle of life, only a principle of life can be a body.
questions.explanation: He argues that a body can be a principle of life, but the first principle (the soul) cannot be a body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 1, that the soul must be a body because it moves the body?
options: He denies that the soul moves the body at all.
He says a mover need not be moved, so the soul can be incorporeal.
He claims the soul is a body because it is the moving principle of the body.
He argues that only bodies can move, so the soul must be a body.
questions.explanation: He replies that a mover need not be moved, so the soul can be incorporeal.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the human soul?
options: The human soul dies when the body dies, like animal souls.
The human soul is a physical form that decays with the body.
The human soul is corruptible because it originates from nothing.
The human soul is immortal and cannot cease to exist.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states that the intellectual principle, or human soul, is incorruptible, distinguishing it from the corruptible souls of animals.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's primary reason for claiming the human soul is incorruptible?
options: It exists independently as a substance, not just as a part of a body.
It is created directly by God without any natural process.
It is made of the same eternal material as the heavenly bodies.
It never interacts with the physical senses or the material world.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that because the human soul is a self-subsistent form (it exists in its own right), it cannot be corrupted accidentally with the body, unlike animal souls which are merely parts of the body.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that the soul needs the body to understand?
options: He argues that understanding does not require any mental images at all.
He claims the soul understands differently after separating from the body.
He denies that the soul ever needs the body for any operation.
He states that the soul stops understanding once the body dies.
questions.explanation: In Reply to Objection 3, Aquinas explains that while understanding through images is the soul's mode of operation while united to the body, it will have a different mode of understanding after separation.

questions.q: What does Aquinas conclude about whether it belongs to man to act for an end?
options: Human actions are never for an end.
No, only some actions are for an end.
Only irrational actions are for an end.
Yes, all human actions are for an end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that all human actions must be for an end.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say all human actions are for an end?
options: Because irrational animals act for ends, so humans must too.
Because the end is always the last step in any action.
Because the end is the first in the agent’s intention, making it a cause.
Because ends are unrelated to human will.
questions.explanation: He argues the end is first in the agent’s intention, thus a cause of the action.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to Objection 3 about actions without deliberation?
options: He says those actions are still human because they have an end.
He says those actions are not truly human, lacking deliberate will.
He says such actions are voluntary and thus human.
He says the end is imaginary but still counts as a human end.
questions.explanation: Aquinas replies that actions without deliberation are not properly human, as they lack a deliberate will.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding human actions?
options: Human actions are voluntary only when God is absent.
Only animals can act voluntarily, not human beings.
There must be some voluntary element in human acts.
Human actions are entirely determined by external forces.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that 'There must needs be something voluntary in human acts,' rejecting the idea that they are purely external.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what specific combination makes an action voluntary?
options: The action is new and not preceded by any previous motion.
The action starts from outside the agent but ends inside the agent.
The agent has an internal drive and understands the goal of the action.
The agent acts without any knowledge of the end or purpose.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that voluntary action requires an intrinsic principle (acting from within) combined with knowledge of the end (purpose), which distinguishes it from mere natural movement.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that humans cannot do anything without God?
options: He says God moves the will itself, which is the first mover.
He argues that God only moves the body, not the will.
He claims that humans can act independently of God's influence.
He states that the biblical quote is misinterpreted in this context.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that God moves the will itself, as every movement proceeds from God as the First Mover, without negating the voluntary nature of the act.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the relationship between charity and friendship?
options: Charity is merely a strong desire for God, similar to loving wine or a horse.
Charity is a form of friendship because it involves wishing good to others based on shared happiness.
Charity is a duty to love enemies, which contradicts the mutual nature of friendship.
Charity is not friendship because God and angels do not live among humans.
questions.explanation: Aquinas concludes that charity is indeed friendship because it is founded on the communication of God's happiness to us, involving mutual love and benevolence.

questions.q: According to Aquinas, what is the essential foundation that makes charity a true friendship?
options: The mutual sharing of happiness, where God communicates His joy to humans.
The strict requirement that friends must never have any disagreements or conflicts.
The expectation of useful benefits or pleasant experiences from the other person.
The physical presence of friends dwelling together in the same location.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that friendship requires a 'communication' or fellowship; since God shares His happiness with us, a friendship based on this sharing exists.

questions.q: How does Aquinas reply to the objection that charity cannot be friendship because we must love our enemies?
options: We love enemies indirectly, out of loyalty to God, just as we love a friend's servants.
Enemies are actually friends in disguise, so loving them is natural and expected.
Charity is not friendship, but a separate virtue that overrides the rules of friendship.
We only pretend to love our enemies to avoid conflict, which is not true friendship.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explains that friendship extends to others for the sake of the primary friend; we love sinners (enemies) for God's sake, similar to how we love a friend's household.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final verdict on the definition of justice as 'the perpetual and constant will to render to each one his right'?
options: He rejects it because only God possesses a truly perpetual will.
He claims it is wrong because justice is a habit, not a will.
He argues it is incomplete because it ignores love of God.
He accepts it as a fitting definition, provided it is understood correctly.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the definition is fitting if understood aright, clarifying that 'will' refers to the voluntary act and the habit is defined by that act.

questions.q: Why does Aquinas say the definition mentions 'will', 'constancy', and 'perpetuity'?
options: To show that just acts must be voluntary, firm, and stable.
To prove that human justice is identical to God's eternal will.
To distinguish justice from other virtues that lack a will.
To emphasize that justice requires legal enforcement by sovereigns.
questions.explanation: He explains that 'will' indicates the act is voluntary, while 'constancy' and 'perpetuity' indicate the firmness and stability required for a virtuous act.

questions.q: How does Aquinas answer the objection that 'perpetual' and 'constant' mean the same thing?
options: 'Perpetual' means intending to be just always; 'constant' means sticking to it.
He argues that 'constant' implies speed, while 'perpetual' implies duration.
'Perpetual' refers to God's will, while 'constant' refers to human effort.
He agrees they are redundant and suggests removing one word.
questions.explanation: In Reply 4, Aquinas distinguishes them: 'perpetual will' denotes the purpose to observe justice always, while 'constant' signifies firm perseverance in that purpose.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding God becoming human?
options: It was impossible because a spirit cannot join with a body.
It was unnecessary because God was already perfect without flesh.
It was fitting for God to become incarnate.
It was unfitting because God is infinite and flesh is finite.
questions.explanation: Aquinas explicitly states in his answer that it was fitting for God to become incarnate because it aligns with the nature of goodness.

questions.q: What is the main reason Aquinas gives for why the Incarnation was fitting?
options: God needed to change His eternal nature to save humanity.
The universe required a physical ruler to manage its affairs.
Goodness naturally communicates itself to others in the highest way.
Human flesh was dignified enough to unite with God naturally.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that since God's nature is goodness, and goodness communicates itself, it is fitting for God to join created nature to Himself.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that God cannot be contained in a small body?
options: God abandoned the universe to focus on governing the human body.
God used the body as a tool to expand the universe's size.
God contracted His power to fit inside the frail human body.
God did not lose or transfer His care of the universe to the body.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the fourth objection, Aquinas cites Augustine to clarify that God did not desert, lose, or contract His care of the universe into the body.

questions.q: What is Aquinas's final conclusion regarding the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist?
options: It is present in a way that can be verified by human reason.
It is present in very truth, though not detectable by senses.
It is present only in a spiritual sense, not physically.
It is present only as a symbolic sign or figure.
questions.explanation: Aquinas argues that Christ's body is present in 'very truth' and not merely as a sign, but this presence is known through faith rather than physical senses or human understanding.

questions.q: What is the primary reason Aquinas gives for why Christ's body must be truly present in the sacrament?
options: To show that Christ's body can be in multiple places at once.
To allow the faithful to see Christ with their physical eyes.
To fulfill the perfection of the New Law and Christ's love for us.
To prove that the Old Law sacrifices were completely wrong.
questions.explanation: Aquinas states that the true presence is necessary for the perfection of the New Law and reflects Christ's love, as He desires to unite with His friends in a familiar way.

questions.q: How does Aquinas respond to the objection that a physical body cannot be in several places at once?
options: He states that angels can be in several places, so Christ can too.
He claims that the objection is based on a misreading of Augustine.
He argues that Christ's body is present in a special, non-spatial manner.
He agrees that the body is not physically present in the sacrament.
questions.explanation: In his reply to the third objection, Aquinas explains that Christ's body is not in the sacrament in the same way a normal body occupies a place, but in a special manner unique to this sacrament.
